1.h: אוֹת א׳ — סְעִיף 1 (הַקְדָּמָה) — Section 1 (Ois Aleph: Introduction)

The theme: The overarching purpose of the mitzvos to sanctify Israel, the commandment of "You shall be holy", and the covenant of moral purity. The author dedicates this treatise, titled Yisrael Kedoshim, to expounding the supreme sanctity of Israel, whom Hashem separated from the nations to be His holy people. All 613 commandments infuse divine holiness into the heart of an Israelite, fulfilling "and do all My commandments, and be holy unto your God" (Bamidbar 15:40) and "Who has sanctified us with His commandments". In Yevamos (20a), the Sages teach that "you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy" (Vayikra 11:44) is an overarching positive commandment embracing all positive and negative precepts, elevating man to resemble his Creator who is holy. The primary locus of holiness resides in guarding the holy covenant (kedushat ha-brit), for wherever a fence against sexual immorality (geder ervah) is found, holiness is present (Vayikra Rabbah 24:6; Rashi on Vayikra 19:2). A Nazirite is called holy because he abstains from wine, wine being an instigator of licentiousness (Sotah 2a, 7a; Berachos 29b). Restraining physical desires—especially the appetite for food ("a full belly breeds evil vices", Berachos 32a)—creates an essential safeguard for moral purity, as Scripture and the Sages frequently employ the euphemism of eating for marital intimacy (Bereishis 39:6; Mishlei 30:20; Kesubos 65b; Shabbat 62b).

p: בְּעֶזְרַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
With the assistance of the Blessed Name.
״אַתָּה חוֹנֵן לְאָדָם דַּעַת, וּמְלַמֵּד לֶאֱנוֹשׁ בִּינָה; חָנֵּנוּ מֵאִתְּךָ חָכְמָה, בִּינָה וָדָעַת״.
"You graciously endow man with knowledge, and teach mortal man understanding; graciously bestow upon us from Yourself wisdom, understanding, and knowledge."
״שִׁוִּיתִי ה׳ לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד״ (תְּהִלִּים ט״ז:ח׳).
"I have set Hashem always before me" (Tehillim 16:8).
״וּבְרוּכִים אַתֶּם לַה׳״.
"And blessed are you unto Hashem."
בְּסִיַּעְתָּא דִּשְׁמַיָּא.
With the help of Heaven.
קוּנְטְרֵס קְרָאתִיו בְּשֵׁם ״יִשְׂרָאֵל קְדוֹשִׁים״
A treatise have I called by the name "Yisrael Kedoshim" [Holy Israel];
מְיוּסָּד עַל תֹּקֶף מַעֲלַת קְדֻשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל, אֲשֶׁר הִבְדִּילָנוּ מִכָּל הָעַמִּים לִהְיוֹת לוֹ לְגוֹי קָדוֹשׁ:
founded upon the supreme excellence of the sanctity of Israel, whom He separated from all the nations to be unto Him a holy nation!
כָּל הַמִּצְוֹת מַכְנִיסוֹת קְדוּשָׁה בְּלֵב אִישׁ יִשְׂרְאֵלִי
All the commandments infuse holiness into the heart of an Israelite man;
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״[לְמַעַן תִּזְכְּרוּ] וַעֲשִׂיתֶם אֶת כָּל מִצְוֹתָי, וִהְיִיתֶם קְדֹשִׁים [לֵאלֹהֵיכֶם]״ (בַּמִּדְבָּר ט״ו:מ׳)
as it is said: "that you may remember, and do all My commandments, and be holy unto your God" (Bamidbar 15:40);
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאוֹמְרִים: ״קַדְּשֵׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתֶיךָ״
and as we say in prayer: "sanctify us with Your commandments";
וּמְבָרְכִין עֲלֵיהֶם: ״אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ״
and we recite the blessing over them: "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us".
נִרְאֶה דְּזֶהוּ הַמְכֻוָּון שֶׁל כָּל הַמִּצְוֹת: לִהְיוֹת עַל יָדָם קְדוֹשִׁים
It appears that this is the primary intent of all the commandments: to become holy through their agency;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּיבָמוֹת (כ׳ עַמּוּד ב׳): דְּ״וְהִתְקַדִּשְׁתֶּם״ (וַיִּקְרָא י״א:מ״ד) הוּא מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה כּוֹלֶלֶת עַל כָּל עֲשֵׂה וְלֹא תַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסָפוֹת

and as the Sages stated in Yevamos (20b): "and you shall sanctify yourselves" (Vayikra 11:44) is an all-inclusive positive commandment embracing every positive and negative precept in the Torah, see Tosafos there;
שֶׁעַל יְדֵיהֶם הָאָדָם מִתְקַדֵּשׁ
for through them man becomes consecrated;
וְזֶהוּ תַּכְלִית בְּרִיאַת הָאָדָם בָּעוֹלָם: לְהִתְדַּמּוֹת אֵלָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ
this being the ultimate purpose of man's creation in the world: to emulate the Blessed One;
שֶׁהוּא קָדוֹשׁ וּמְשָׁרְתָיו קְדוֹשִׁים, וְנֶאֱמַר: ״קְדֹשִׁים תִּהְיוּ, כִּי קָדוֹשׁ אֲנִי [ה׳ אֱלֹהֵיכֶם]״ (וַיִּקְרָא י״ט:ב׳)
for He is holy and His ministering attendants are holy, and it is said: "You shall be holy, for I Hashem your God am holy" (Vayikra 19:2).
וְעִיקַּר הַקְּדוּשָׁה הוּא קְדֻשַּׁת הַבְּרִית
And the essential core of holiness is the holiness of the covenant;
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה כ״ד:ו׳): ״כָּל מָקוֹם שֶׁאַתָּה מוֹצֵא גֶּדֶר עֶרְוָה — אַתָּה מוֹצֵא קְדוּשָׁה״
as the Sages taught in Vayikra Rabbah (24:6): "Wherever you find a fence against sexual immorality, you find holiness";
כִּדְאָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן פָּזִי: ״כָּל שֶׁהוּא גּוֹדֵר עַצְמוֹ מִן הָעֶרְוָה — נִקְרָא קָדוֹשׁ״, עַיֵּין שָׁם וּבְרַשִׁ״י רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת קְדוֹשִׁים
as Rabbi Yehudah ben Pazi stated: "Whoever erects a fence around himself against immorality is called holy," see there and in Rashi at the beginning of Parashat Kedoshim;
וּבַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי פֶּרֶק ב׳ דִּיבָמוֹת הֲלָכָה ד׳: ״כָּל מִי שֶׁפּוֹרֵשׁ עַצְמוֹ מֵהָעֲרָיוֹת וְכוּלֵיהּ״
and in the Jerusalem Talmud (Yevamos 2:4): "Whoever separates himself from illicit relations, etc.";
וּבְשַׁבָּת (קי״ח עַמּוּד ב׳): ״מַאי טַעְמָא קְרוֹ לָךְ רַבֵּינוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ? ...לֹא נִסְתַּכַּלְתִּי... שֶׁלֹּא הִכְנִיס וְכוּלֵיהּ״
and in Shabbat (118b): "Why do they call you 'our holy Master'? ...Because I never gazed upon my circumcised flesh, nor placed my hand below my belt, etc."
וְהַנָּזִיר נִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן בַּתּוֹרָה ״קָדוֹשׁ״ (בַּמִּדְבָּר ו:ה)
And the Nazirite is likewise called "holy" in the Torah (Bamidbar 6:5);
וְעִיקָּרוֹ לְפִי שֶׁנָּזַר עַצְמוֹ מִן הַיַּיִן, שֶׁהוּא גֶּדֶר עֶרְוָה, דְּ״הַרְבֵּה יַיִן עוֹשֶׂה״, כִּדִתְנַן בְּסוֹטָה (ז׳ עַמּוּד א׳)
and the essence of his sanctity is because he abstains from wine, which serves as a fence against immorality, for "wine accomplishes much," as taught in Sotah (7a);
וְשָׁם (ב׳ עַמּוּד א׳): ״הָרוֹאֶה סוֹטָה בְּקִלְקוּלָהּ — יַזִּיר עַצְמוֹ מִן הַיַּיִן״
and there (2a): "Whoever sees a suspected adulteress in her degradation should take a vow of Naziriteship from wine";
וּבִבְרָכוֹת (כ״ט עַמּוּד ב׳): ״לָא תִּרְוֵי וְלָא תֶחֱטֵי״
and in Berachos (29b): "Do not become intoxicated and you will not sin";
וְכֵן גִּידּוּל הַפֶּרַע לְגַלְּחוֹ לַשָּׁמַיִם מַצִּיל מִפַּחֲזוּת הַיֵּצֶר בְּהִרְהוּרִים
and likewise letting the hair grow wild to shave it for Heaven saves man from the recklessness of the yetzer in unholy lustful thoughts;
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעוּבְדָא דְּנָזִיר (נָדָרִים ט׳ עַמּוּד ב׳), עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י
as the Sages recounted in the incident of the handsome shepherd who became a Nazirite (Nedarim 9b), see Rashi there;
וּבִבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה פ״ז (סִימָן ג׳): בְּיוֹסֵף: ״מְתַקֵּן בִּשְׂעָרוֹ וְכוּלֵיהּ, הָא דּוּבָּא קַמָּךְ״
and in Bereishis Rabbah (87:3) regarding Joseph: "curling his hair, etc.—behold, the bear is set before you" [Potiphar's wife].
וּבִכְלַל זֶה כָּל הַגְדָּרוֹת תַּאֲווֹת הַגּוּפָנִיּוֹת הֵם גֶּדֶר לָעֶרְוָה
And included within this, all restraints placed upon bodily lusts serve as an indispensable fence against sexual immorality;
וְעַל כֵּן לְחַד מַאן דְּאָמַר בְּתַעֲנִית (י״א עַמּוּד א׳): ״הַיּוֹשֵׁב בְּתַעֲנִית — נִקְרָא קָדוֹשׁ״
wherefore according to one authority in Ta'anit (11a): "One who sits in fasting is called holy";
״מַה זֶּה שֶׁצִּיעֵר עַצְמוֹ מִדָּבָר אֶחָד נִקְרָא קָדוֹשׁ, הַמְצַעֵר עַצְמוֹ מִכָּל דָּבָר עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה״
"if a Nazirite who denied himself only one thing is called holy, one who fasts and denies himself all food and drink how much more so!"
וּמִתַּאֲוַת אֲכִילָה בְּיִחוּד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (ל״ב עַמּוּד א׳): ״מָלֵי כְּרֵיסֵי — זַנֵּי בִּישֵׁי״
And specifically restraint from the lust for food, as stated in Berachos (32a): "a full belly breeds evil vices";
וְכֵן נִקְרָא בִּלְשׁוֹן אֲכִילָה: ״אָכְלָה וּמָחֲתָה פִיהָ״ (מִשְׁלֵי ל:כ)
and so intimacy is termed with the idiom of eating: "she eats, and wipes her mouth" (Mishlei 30:20);
וּבִלְשׁוֹן מִשְׁנָה: ״אוֹכֶלֶת עִמּוֹ לֵילֵי שַׁבָּת״ (כְּתוּבּוֹת ס״ה עַמּוּד ב׳) לְחַד מַאן דְּאָמַר
and in the language of the Mishnah: "she eats with him on Friday nights" (Kesubos 65b) according to one opinion [euphemism for marital relations];
וּבִלְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם (שַׁבָּת ס״ב סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳): ״בַּמֶּה סָעַדְתָּ?״ וְכוּלֵיהּ
and in the vernacular of mortals (Shabbat 62b): "Upon what did you dine today?";
וְגַם בִּלְשׁוֹן תּוֹרָה לְפִי הַבְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה פ״ו:ח׳) עַל פָּסוּק ״כִּי אִם הַלֶּחֶם אֲשֶׁר הוּא אוֹכֵל״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית ל״ט:ו׳): לְשׁוֹן נָקִי:
and also in the biblical text according to Bereishis Rabbah (86:8) on "save the bread which he did eat" (Bereishis 39:6): an elevated euphemism for marital intimacy!

1.h: אוֹת א׳ — סְעִיפִים 2–3 (מֹשֶׁה, אֵלִיָּהוּ, וֶאֱלִישָׁע) — Sections 2–3 (Ois Aleph: Moshe, Eliyahu, Elisha, and the Shunammite)

The theme: The interrelation of food and carnal desire, and Elisha designated as a "holy man" by the Shunammite. The lust for food and carnal lust are inextricably bound. Therefore, when Moshe Rabbeinu separated from his wife from the Giving of the Torah onward, he was simultaneously empowered to fast forty days and forty nights without food or drink (Shemos 34:28). Similarly, Eliyahu—the angel of the covenant—fasted forty days (I Melachim 19:8), sustained by the bread of Torah: "Come, eat of my bread" (Mishlei 9:5). His disciple Elisha, although not transformed into an angel like his master, attained the absolute pinnacle of human holiness, meriting to be designated a "holy man of God" by the Shunammite woman (II Melachim 4:9; Berachos 10b). The woman recognized his holiness because the root of carnal lust was concentrated in the woman, who brought death to the world through the Serpent's seduction; the knowledge of evil gained from the Tree of Knowledge enables one to discern the corresponding heights of the good. The Gemara asks: How did the Shunammite know Elisha was holy? One Sage answers that she never saw a fly upon his table—perceiving through his eating that he was completely devoid of the yetzer hara, which is likened unto a fly (Berachos 61a), and knowing that one who controls food controls sexual desire. Another Sage answers that she never saw a nocturnal emission upon his linen sheets, even though the exertion of travel often brings about emission even in the pious (Shabbat 127b). Complete protection from involuntary bodily impurities cannot be achieved by mortal effort alone, but is granted from Above in proportion to how one sanctifies himself below (Yoma 39a).

p: וּשְׁנֵי תַּאֲווֹת אֵלּוּ — הָא בְּהָא תַּלְיָין
And these two physical desires—food and immorality—are mutually dependent upon each other;
וְעַל כֵּן מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, מִשֶּׁפֵּירַשׁ מִן הָאִשָּׁה מִמַּתַּן תּוֹרָה וָאֵילָךְ
wherefore Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, once he separated from his wife from the Giving of the Torah onward;
זָכָה גַּם כֵּן לִהְיוֹת אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם בְּלֹא אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה (שְׁמוֹת ל״ד:כ״ח)
merited likewise to endure forty days without eating and drinking (Shemos 34:28);
וְכֵן אֵלִיָּהוּ שֶׁנִּקְרָא ״מַלְאַךְ הַבְּרִית״ (מַלְאָכִי ג:א; פִּרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר כ״ט), גַּם כֵּן אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם (מְלָכִים א י״ט:ח׳)
and so Eliyahu who is called the "angel of the covenant," likewise fasted forty days (I Melachim 19:8);
שֶׁהוּא הַשִּׁיעוּר שֶׁל קַבָּלַת הַתּוֹרָה, דְּעַל יָדָהּ הָיוּ נִיזוֹנִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״לְכוּ לַחֲמוּ בְלַחֲמִי וְגוֹמֵר״ (מִשְׁלֵי ט:ה)
which is the required measure for receiving the Torah, through which they were spiritually nourished: "Come, eat of my bread, etc." (Mishlei 9:5).
וֶאֱלִישָׁע תַּלְמִיד אֵלִיָּהוּ וְהוֹלֵךְ בְּעִקְּבוֹתָיו
And Elisha, the disciple of Eliyahu who walked in his footsteps;
אַף שֶׁלֹּא זָכָה לְהִתְקַדֵּשׁ כִּמְלָאכִים מַמָּשׁ וּלְהִתְהַפֵּךְ לְמַלְאָךְ כְּרַבּוֹ
although he did not merit to become consecrated as an actual angel or be transformed into an angel like his master;
שֶׁזֶּה לֹא זָכָה לָהּ אָדָם בָּעוֹלָם חוּץ מֵאֵלִיָּהוּ מִצַּד שָׁרְשׁוֹ
which level no mortal in the world ever achieved save Eliyahu by virtue of his soul-root;
מִכָּל מָקוֹם נִתְקַדֵּשׁ בְּתַכְלִית הַקְּדוּשָׁה הָאֶפְשָׁרִית בַּאֲנָשִׁים בַּאֲשֶׁר הוּא אָדָם
nevertheless Elisha sanctified himself to the utmost boundary of holiness possible for human beings;
וְזָכָה לִיקָּרֵא בְּשֵׁם ״אִישׁ קָדוֹשׁ״ (מְלָכִים ב ד:ט) עַל יְדֵי הָאִשָּׁה הַמַּכֶּרֶת בְּאוֹרְחִים יוֹתֵר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (י׳ עַמּוּד ב׳)
and merited to be designated a "holy man" (II Melachim 4:9) through the Shunammite woman who discerns the character of guests more than a man (Berachos 10b).
כִּי עִיקַּר כֹּחַ הַתַּאֲוָה בָּאִשָּׁה, שֶׁהֵבִיאָה עַל יְדֵי זֶה מִיתָה לָעוֹלָם
For the primary seat of physical desire was in the woman, who brought death to the world through it;
וּתְחִלַּת הַסָּתַת הַנָּחָשׁ הָיָה בָהּ וְהִטִּיל בָּהּ זוּהֲמָא (שַׁבָּת קמ״ו עַמּוּד א׳)
the initial seduction of the Serpent having targeted her, injecting into her unholy defilement (Shabbat 146a);
וְהָרָע מַבְחִין אֶת הַטּוֹב
and experiential knowledge of evil enables the sharp perception of the good;
וּמִצַּד תַּעֲרוֹבֶת יְדִיעַת טוֹב וָרָע שֶׁעַל יְדֵי אֲכִילַת עֵץ הַדַּעַת
and through the mixture of good and evil born from eating of the Tree of Knowledge;
כְּפִי גּוֹדֶל הַיְּדִיעָה בָּרָע — כֵּן גּוֹדֶל הַיְּדִיעָה בַּטּוֹב, ״זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה״ (קֹהֶלֶת ז:יד)
matching the depth of knowledge of evil is the capacity to discern the good, "one opposite the other" (Koheles 7:14).
וְאָמְרוּ שָׁם: ״מְנָא יָדְעָה?״ (בְּרָכוֹת י׳ עַמּוּד ב׳)
And the Talmud asked there: "From where did she know that Elisha was a holy man?" (Berachos 10b);
כִּי קְדֻשַּׁת הַבְּרִית מִדְּבָרִים שֶׁבְּצִנְעָה שֶׁאֵין נִיכָּר
for the holiness of the covenant belongs to hidden matters that are not visibly evident;
וְחַד אָמַר: ״שֶׁלֹּא רָאֲתָה זְבוּב עַל שֻׁלְחָנוֹ״
and one Sage answered: "she never saw a fly pass over his table";
הַיְינוּ שֶׁהִכִּירָה בַּאֲכִילָתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בְּתַאֲוַת הַיֵּצֶר הַנִּמְשָׁל לִזְבוּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם ס״א סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳)
meaning she perceived through his eating that he possessed no lust of the yetzer hara, which is likened unto a fly (Berachos 61a);
וּמִזֶּה יָדְעָה שֶׁגָּדוּר בַּעֲרָיוֹת גַּם כֵּן
and from his restraint in food she deduced that he was fenced against carnal immorality as well;
וְחַד אָמַר: ״סָדִין שֶׁל פִּשְׁתָּן הִצִּיעָה לוֹ, וְלֹא רָאֲתָה קֶרִי עָלָיו״
and another Sage answered: "she spread a sheet of white linen, and never saw a nocturnal emission upon it";
אַף שֶׁטּוֹרַח הַדֶּרֶךְ מֵבִיא לִידֵי קֶרִי גַּם לַחֲסִידִים פְּעָמִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (קכ״ז עַמּוּד ב׳)
even though the weariness of travel induces seminal emission sometimes even in the pious (Shabbat 127b).
וְדָבָר זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לָאָדָם לְהִזָּהֵר בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא יֶאֱרַע
And from such involuntary bodily occurrences man cannot protect himself through mortal striving alone;
רַק מַה שֶּׁשּׁוֹמְרִין אוֹתוֹ מִלְּמַעְלָה כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁמַּקְדִּישׁ עַצְמוֹ מִלְּמַטָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (ל״ט עַמּוּד א׳)
but only through being guarded from Above in proportion to how one sanctifies himself below (Yoma 39a);
וּמִי שֶׁמִּתְקַדֵּשׁ לְמַטָּה בְּתַכְלִית כֹּחַ הָאֱנוֹשִׁי, כֵּן מְקַדְּשִׁין אוֹתוֹ מִלְּמַעְלָה בְּתַכְלִית כֹּחַ הָאֱלֹהִי שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שִׁיעוּר
and whoever consecrates himself below to the utmost limit of human capacity, Heaven sanctifies him with boundless divine energy;
וְנִיצּוֹל גַּם מִטֻּמְאוֹת הַמּוּכְרָחוֹת בְּטֶבַע הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה:
being miraculously preserved even from involuntary bodily impurities natural to this world!

1.h: אוֹת א׳ — סְעִיף 4 (הַסֻּלָּם שֶׁל רַבִּי פִּנְחָס בֶּן יָאִיר) — Section 4 (Ois Aleph: The Ladder of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair)

The theme: The mitzvos as divine strategies to draw down holiness, and the progressive ladder of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair. All 613 commandments are divine counsels (eitin) and assistances from Hashem to draw supernal holiness down upon man. Thus the Sages expound in Avodah Zarah (20b) on "and you shall keep yourself from every evil thing" (Devarim 23:10): that a man should not entertain unholy thoughts by day that lead to impurity by night. From this, Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair formulated the progressive ladder: "Torah brings to watchfulness (zehirut), watchfulness brings to zeal (zerizut)... leading ultimately unto holiness (kedushah) and the Holy Spirit". Although the Baraita concludes that "piety (chasidut) is the greatest of them all," there is no contradiction: piety is the supreme quality of the soul, but in terms of embodied human attainment, holiness is the final rung, for subduing and purifying the physical body is the heaviest task, achievable only after passing through all preceding rungs. When man guards the boundaries of Torah and sanctifies himself below, Heaven guards him from nocturnal impurity beyond his control, crowning him as an authentic "holy man" (ish kadosh).

p: וְכָל הַמִּצְוֹת עֲשֵׂה וְלֹא תַעֲשֶׂה הֵם סַיַּיעְתּוֹת וְעֵצוֹת מִגְּדוֹל הָעֵצָה יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ, לְהָבִיא עַל הָאָדָם הַקְּדוּשָׁה מִלְּמַעְלָה
And all the positive and negative commandments are divine assistances and counsels from the Master of Counsel, blessed be His Name, to draw holiness upon man from on High;
וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (כ׳ עַמּוּד ב׳): ״׳וְנִשְׁמַרְתָּ מִכֹּל דָּבָר רָע׳ (דְּבָרִים כ״ג:י׳) — שֶׁלֹּא יְהַרְהֵר אָדָם בַּיּוֹם וְיָבוֹא לִידֵי קֶרִי בַּלַּיְלָה״

wherefore the Sages taught in Avodah Zarah (20b): "'and you shall keep yourself from every evil thing' (Devarim 23:10)—that a man should not harbor lustful thoughts by day and incur impurity by night";
מִכָּאן אָמַר רַבִּי פִּנְחָס בֶּן יָאִיר: ״תּוֹרָה מְבִיאָה לִידֵי זְהִירוּת, זְהִירוּת מְבִיאָה לִידֵי זְרִיזוּת... עַד לִידֵי קְדוּשָׁה״
from here Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair derived: "Torah brings to watchfulness, watchfulness brings to zeal... culminating unto holiness";
כְּפִי הַנּוּסְחָא שֶׁלָּנוּ שֶׁהִיא הָאַחֲרוֹנָה
according to our talmudic text, where holiness is the ultimate rung;
אַף דִּמְסַיֵּים ״וַחֲסִידוּת גְּדוֹלָה מִכּוּלָּן״, אֵין בָּזֶה סְתִירָה
and although the Baraita concludes: "and piety is the greatest of them all," there is no contradiction.
דְּהָךְ ״גְּדוֹלָה״ הַיְינוּ בְּמַעֲלַת הַנֶּפֶשׁ
For that "greatness" of piety refers to the intrinsic virtue of the soul;
אֲבָל לְעִנְיַן הַשָּׂגַת הָאָדָם הַמַּדְרֵיגוֹת מִצַּד מַה שֶּׁהוּא מְלוּבָּשׁ בַּגּוּף, הַקְּדוּשָׁה מְאוּחֶרֶת מִכּוּלָּם
but regarding man's actualized attainment while clothed in a physical body, holiness is the final rung of all;
כִּי כְּבֵידָה עַל הַגּוּף, אִם לֹא אַחַר שֶׁיִּזְדַּכֵּךְ בְּכָל מַדְרֵיגוֹת הַקּוֹדְמוֹת
for physical purification weighs heavily on the body, unattainable except after being refined through all preceding stages;
וְאַף שֶׁעִיקַּר הֶחָזוֹן נִמְשָׁךְ מִמַּדְרֵיגַת הַחֲסִידוּת
and although divine vision issues primarily from piety;
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא מִתְאַחֵר בְּסֵדֶר זְמַנִּים לָבוֹא, עַד שֶׁיְּזוּכַּךְ גַּם הַגּוּף וְיַגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵיגַת הַקְּדוּשָׁה
nevertheless it arrives late in temporal order, until the physical frame is thoroughly purged and attains holiness.
וְלָמַד זֶה מִקְּרָא דְּ״וְנִשְׁמַרְתָּ״
And Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair derived this from the verse "and you shall keep yourself";
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי שְׁמִירַת גִּדְרֵי הַתּוֹרָה וּקְדֻשָּׁתוֹ מִלְּמַטָּה, שׁוֹמְרִין אוֹתוֹ מִלְּמַעְלָה מִטֻּמְאוֹת שֶׁבְּעֵת שֵׁינָה שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּיָדוֹ
for through observing the fences of Torah and sanctifying oneself below, Heaven protects him from nocturnal impurities during sleep which are beyond his control;
שֶׁזֶּהוּ תַּכְלִית הַקְּדוּשָׁה: לִהְיוֹת ״אִישׁ קָדוֹשׁ״
this being the ultimate purpose of holiness: to become a "holy man";
הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מֵהַתּוֹרָה שֶׁהִיא הַהַתְחָלָה, וּמְבִיאָתוֹ מִמַּדְרֵיגָה לְמַדְרֵיגָה עַד הַקְּדוּשָׁה וְרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ:
descending from the Torah which is the beginning, elevating man step by step unto holiness and the Holy Spirit!

2.h: אוֹת ב׳ — סְעִיפִים 1–2 (קַדֵּשׁ עַצְמְךָ בַּמּוּתָּר לָךְ) — Sections 1–2 (Ois Bet: Sanctify Yourself in the Permissible, Gehazi, and Elisha's Gaze)

The theme: Sanctifying oneself in the permissible (kadesh atzmecha b'mutar lach), Gehazi grabbing the Shunammite, and Elisha withholding his gaze. The essence of holiness is: "Sanctify yourself in that which is permitted to you" (Yevamos 20a), for one who merely refrains from biblical prohibitions is not called "holy," but merely not a "wicked man". In Berachos (10b), the Sages state: "Elisha is holy, but his servant Gehazi is not holy, for he seized the Shunammite between her breasts" (II Melachim 4:27). Gehazi did not intentionally grab her for physical pleasure, for that would make him an outright wicked man (like one who counts coins into a woman's hand, Eruvin 18b); rather, when pushing her away, his hand inadvertently touched her, an accidental mishap that never befalls an authentically holy master. Another Sage in Vayikra Rabbah (24:6) and Yerushalmi Yevamos (2:4) explains that Elisha was called holy because he never looked at the Shunammite. The Magen Avraham (128:35) distinguishes between casual looking (habatah) and lustful gazing (histaklut); yet even casual accidental looking is avoided by a holy man, who averts his eyes even when turning a street corner, just as the pious avert their eyes when women wash garments by the riverbank (Bava Batra 57b; Avodah Zarah 20a). Although in biblical Hebrew habatah denotes intentional looking (Rashi on Bamidbar 21:8), rabbinic Hebrew uses the term differently. Observing rabbinic prohibitions does not yet make one "holy" in the ultimate sense (Yevamos 20a), for an aveirah d'rabbanan is legally binding and its violator is termed wicked; yet rabbinic enactments are called "prohibitions of holiness" (issurei kedushah) because the Sages originally prohibited that which was biblically permitted in order to sanctify the hearts of Israel.

p: וְעִיקַּר הַקְּדוּשָׁה: ״קַדֵּשׁ עַצְמְךָ בַּמֻּתָּר לָךְ״ (יְבָמוֹת כ׳ עַמּוּד א׳)
And the primary essence of holiness is: "Sanctify yourself in that which is permitted to you" (Yevamos 20a);
דְּדָבָר הָאָסוּר, מַאן דְּלָא עָבֵיד הָכִי — ״רָשָׁע״ נַמֵּי מִקְרֵי, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם)
for regarding a forbidden thing, he who does not observe it is designated a "wicked man" (ibid.).
וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (י׳ עַמּוּד ב׳): ״[אִישׁ אֱלֹהִים קָדוֹשׁ הוּא] — וּמְשָׁרְתוֹ אֵינוֹ קָדוֹשׁ, שֶׁאֲחָזָהּ [בְּהוֹד יוֹפְיָהּ] וְכוּלֵיהּ״
And one must understand what the Sages expounded in Berachos (10b): "'Elisha is a holy man of God'—but his servant is not holy, for he seized the Shunammite by her physical beauty, etc.";
לֹא שֶׁאֲחָזָהּ בְּמִתְכַּוֵּון לַהֲנָאָתוֹ
not that Gehazi grabbed her intentionally for physical pleasure;
דְּהַהוּא לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ שֶׁאֵינוֹ קָדוֹשׁ, דַּאֲפִילּוּ ״רָשָׁע״ נַמֵּי מִקְרֵי
for in that case the term "not holy" would not apply, seeing that he would be designated an outright "wicked man";
דַּאֲפִילּוּ: ״הַמַּרְצֶה מָעוֹת [מִיָּדוֹ לְיָדָהּ כְּדֵי לְהִסְתַּכֵּל בָּהּ] וְכוּלֵיהּ״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (י״ח עַמּוּד ב׳)
for even counting out coins directly into a woman's hand to gaze at her is sinful, as stated in Eruvin (18b);
אֶלָּא שֶׁכְּשֶׁבָּא לְהָדְפָהּ נִזְדַּמֵּן שֶׁאֲחָזָהּ וְכוּלֵיהּ
but when he came to push her away, his hand inadvertently touched her;
וּלְמִי שֶׁהוּא קָדוֹשׁ לֹא יִזְדַּמֵּן כָּךְ
and unto one who is authentically holy such a physical mishap never occurs!
וּמַה שֶּׁאָמַר חַד מַאן דְּאָמַר בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה כ״ד:ו׳) וּבַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי (פֶּרֶק ב׳ דִּיבָמוֹת הֲלָכָה ד׳): ״אִישׁ קָדוֹשׁ הוּא — שֶׁלֹּא הִבִּיט בָּהּ״
And what one authority states in Vayikra Rabbah (24:6) and Yerushalmi Yevamos (2:4): "he is a holy man—because he never gazed upon her";
אוּלַי יֵשׁ לְחַלֵּק בֵּין ״הַבָּטָה״ לִ״הִסְתַּכְּלוּת״ הָאָסוּר בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (כ׳ סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳)
perhaps one might distinguish between casual looking (habatah) and lustful gazing (histaklut) forbidden in Avodah Zarah (20a);
עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּמָגֵן אַבְרָהָם (סִימָן קכ״ח סָעִיף קָטָן ל״ה), עַיֵּין שָׁם
after the manner written by the Magen Avraham (128:35), see there;
אַךְ לְפִי זֶה מַאי פָּרִיךְ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שָׁם אַדְּרַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל דְּרָאָה וְכוּלֵיהּ
yet if so, why did the Gemara challenge Rabban Gamliel who merely looked at a beautiful woman (Avodah Zarah 20a);
וְעַל כָּרְחָךְ דְּכָל רְאִיָּה בְּעָלְמָא גַּם כֵּן אָסוּר
proving perforce that even casual looking is forbidden!
וְצָרִיךְ לְפָרֵשׁ הָךְ ״הַבָּטָה״ עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם (בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כ׳ רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳) אַדְּרַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל: ״קֶרֶן זָוִית הֲוַאי״
And one must interpret this casual looking after the manner answered regarding Rabban Gamliel: "it was a sudden blind street corner";
וְאִישׁ קָדוֹשׁ עוֹצֵם עֵינָיו בִּכְהַאי גַּוְונָא דְּאָנִיס גַּם כֵּן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (נ״ז עַמּוּד ב׳)
and a holy man shuts his eyes even in an accidental encounter, as stated in Bava Batra (57b);
וְשָׁם כְּשֶׁעוֹמְדוֹת עַל הַכְּבִיסָה: זֶה גַּם רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל עָבֵיד
and where women stand washing garments, closing one's eyes is performed by Rabban Gamliel as well;
אֲבָל בִּפְנִיָּה בְּעָלְמָא וְשֶׁלֹּא בְּכַוָּונָה הִיא קְדוּשָׁה יְתֵירָה דַּחֲזָיָה בֵּיהּ בֶּאֱלִישָׁע
but averting the eyes even on a casual turn without intent was the extraordinary holiness seen in Elisha;
וְאַף דִּבִלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב ״הַבָּטָה״ הִיא בְּכַוָּונָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁפֵּירֵשׁ רַשִׁ״י (פָּרָשַׁת חֻקַּת כ״א:ח׳)
and though in biblical Hebrew habatah denotes intentional looking (Rashi on Bamidbar 21:8);
לְשׁוֹן תּוֹרָה לְחוּד וּלְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים לְחוּד (חֻלִּין קל״ז עַמּוּד ב׳):
the language of the Torah is distinct from the language of the Sages (Chullin 137b)!
וְאַף אִיסּוּרִין דְּרַבָּנַן לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ לִקְרוֹת הַמְקַיֵּים ״קָדוֹשׁ״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר רָבָא בִּיבָמוֹת שָׁם (כ׳ עַמּוּד א׳)
And regarding rabbinic prohibitions it is likewise inappropriate to designate one who observes them as "holy," as Rava stated in Yevamos (20a);
וּמַה דְּמַסִּיק מִכָּל מָקוֹם דְּ״אִיסּוּר קְדוּשָׁה״ רָצָה לוֹמַר אִיסּוּרִין דְּרַבָּנַן דְּ״קַדֵּשׁ עַצְמְךָ בַּמֻּתָּר לָךְ״
and when the Gemara concludes that "prohibitions of holiness" denote rabbinic enactments of sanctifying oneself in the permitted;
הַכַּוָּונָה: דִּנְהִי דְּאַחַר שֶׁגָּזְרוּ חֲכָמִים שׁוּב הוּא עָלֵינוּ כְּכָל אִיסּוּרִין דְּהָעוֹבֵר נִקְרָא ״רָשָׁע״
the meaning is: granted that once the Sages enacted the decree it is binding like all prohibitions and the violator is called wicked;
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הָאִיסּוּר מִצַּד עַצְמוֹ, מִצַּד תְּחִלַּת תַּקָּנַת חֲכָמִים שֶׁהָיָה עַדַיִין הֶיתֵּר
nevertheless the prohibition from its own inception, when it was still biblically permitted;
וַחֲכָמִים בָּאוּ לְאָסְרוֹ, שֶׁהֵם כִּוְּונוּ בָּזֶה לִגְדּוֹר וּלְקַדֵּשׁ בַּמֻּתָּר כְּדֵי לְהוֹסִיף קְדוּשָׁה בְּלִבְּבוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
and the Sages prohibited it aiming to fence and sanctify the permitted to add holiness to the hearts of Israel;
יֵשׁ לִקְרָאוֹ ״אִיסּוּר קְדוּשָׁה״, שֶׁעַל כֵּן אֲסָרוּהוּ כְּדֵי לְהוֹסִיף קְדוּשָׁה בַּמֻּתָּר
it is fittingly called a "prohibition of holiness," instituted to sanctify that which was permitted;
וְאַף אִיסּוּרֵי תוֹרָה, תְּחִלַּת צִוּוּיָן שֶׁהָיָה עַדַיִין הֶיתֵּר וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אֲסָרָן, הָיָה בִּשְׁבִיל כֵּן לְקַדֵּשׁ אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל:
and even biblical prohibitions, at their initial command when they were still permitted and Hashem prohibited them, were given to sanctify Israel!

2.h: אוֹת ב׳ — סְעִיפִים 3–4 (מַחֲלוֹקֶת רַשִׁ״י וְרַמְבַּ״ן, וּדְבָרָיו שֶׁל רַבֵּינוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ) — Sections 3–4 (Ois Bet: Rashi vs. Ramban, and the Levels of Sanctity)

The theme: Reconciling Rashi and the Ramban on "You shall be holy", and the ascending rungs of sanctity up to Rabbeinu HaKadosh. On the verse "You shall be holy" (Vayikra 19:2), Rashi explains: "Be separated from sexual immorality and from transgressions". The Ramban disagrees, arguing that the verse does not address explicit biblical prohibitions (which are commanded elsewhere), but demands self-restraint in permissible food, drink, and intimacy—not becoming a "scoundrel with the Torah's permission" (naval bi-rshut ha-Torah). The Mizrachi noted a contradiction between Vayikra Rabbah and Torat Kohanim; yet the Gemara in Yevamos (20a) explicitly supports the Ramban, for even according to Abaye, one who merely observes biblical law is not termed "holy". Vayikra Rabbah does not dispute Torat Kohanim, for a "fence" (geder) everywhere denotes additional hedges surrounding the core prohibition, like a fence around a vineyard (Chullin 110a; Berachos 22a; Shabbat 16a). Rashi’s view is reconciled by understanding that relative to the pagan nations of the world, collective Israel is called "holy" merely by accepting the Torah: "Israel is holy unto Hashem, the first-fruits of His increase" (Yirmiyah 2:3). Within Israel, relative to lawless rebels who violate rabbinic ordinances, one who observes rabbinic fences is called "holy" (Abaye's view). Among observant, upright Jews, one who fences himself within permissible physical pleasures is called "holy" (Rava and Ramban). Among those who practice self-restraint, one who fences himself with extraordinary stringencies is called "holy" relative to other ascetics—as Elisha was called a "holy man" amidst the generation of prophets, and Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi (Rabbeinu HaKadosh) was singled out among the Tannaim (Shabbat 118b). In Rebbe’s day, there existed the "Holy Congregation of Jerusalem" (Kehilla Kedosha d'vi-Yerushalayim, Yoma 69a; Beitzah 27a); yet Rebbe was crowned "holy" even among that holy assembly. Holiness consists of ascending gradations, mirroring the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies in the Sanctuary!

p: וְזֶהוּ שֶׁכָּתַב רַשִׁ״י רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת קְדוֹשִׁים לְפָרֵשׁ: ״׳קְדֹשִׁים תִּהְיוּ׳ — הֱווּ פְּרוּשִׁים מִן הָעֲרָיוֹת וּמִן הָעֲבֵירָה״
And this explains why Rashi at the beginning of Parashat Kedoshim explains: "'You shall be holy'—be separated from illicit relations and from transgression";
וְהָרַמְבַּ״ן חָלַק עָלָיו: דְּאֵין מְדַבֵּר כָּאן מֵעֲבֵירוֹת הָאֲסוּרוֹת, עַיֵּין שָׁם
and the Ramban disagreed with him: arguing that the verse does not speak here of explicitly forbidden transgressions, see there;
וּבְהָרְאֵ״ם (רַבִּי אֵלִיָּהוּ מִזְרָחִי) שָׁם כָּתַב: דְּלֹא יָדַע לָמָּה נָטָה מִפֵּירוּשׁוֹ, וְשָׁם מַחֲלוֹקֶת בֵּין הַמִּדְרָשׁ וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה לְתוֹרַת כֹּהֲנִים, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם
and the Mizrachi wrote that he did not know why the Ramban departed from Rashi, noting a dispute between Vayikra Rabbah and Torat Kohanim, see there.
וְנִרְאֶה דְּאִשְׁתְּמִיטֵיהּ גְּמָרָא דִּיבָמוֹת הַנִּזְכָּר דִּמְסַיֵּיעַ לְהָרַמְבַּ״ן
And it appears that the aforementioned passage in Yevamos was overlooked, which directly supports the Ramban;
וּמִשָּׁם לָקַח זֶה, דְּאַף לְאַבַּיֵּי שָׁם: רַק הַמְקַיֵּים דִּבְרֵי חֲכָמִים נִקְרָא ״קָדוֹשׁ״
and from there the Ramban took his ruling: that even according to Abaye, only one who observes the words of the Sages is called "holy";
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַב הַמַּגִּיד פֶּרֶק א׳ מֵאִישׁוּת הֲלָכָה ד׳: דְּאִיסּוּרֵי דְּרַבָּנַן כּוּלְּהוּ אִינָשֵׁי לָא זְהִירֵי בְּהוּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם
as the Maggid Mishneh writes (Hilchos Ishut 1:4): that common people are not scrupulous regarding rabbinic enactments, see there;
אֲבָל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה לְכוּלֵי עָלְמָא לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ לִקְרוֹת ״קָדוֹשׁ״
but one who merely refrains from biblical prohibitions is not called "holy" according to all authorities;
וְהַמִּדְרָשׁ וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה הַנַּזְכָּר לְעֵיל לָא פָּלֵיג אַתּוֹרַת כֹּהֲנִים
and Vayikra Rabbah does not dispute Torat Kohanim;
דְּאַדְּרַבָּא גַּם הוּא מְסַיֵּיעַ לְהָרַמְבַּ״ן דְּדָיֵיק בְּלִישָׁנֵיהּ: ״גֶּדֶר עֶרְוָה — כָּל שֶׁגּוֹדֵר עַצְמוֹ וְכוּלֵיהּ״
for on the contrary it supports the Ramban, emphasizing in its wording: "a fence around immorality—whoever fences himself, etc.";
וּבְכָל מָקוֹם ״גֶּדֶר״ הַיְינוּ הַגְדָּרוֹת מוֹסִיפוֹת עַל גּוּף הָאִיסּוּר, שֶׁבּוֹדֵל וּפוֹרֵשׁ עַצְמוֹ מִכָּל סְבִיבוֹתָיו גַּם כֵּן
and everywhere a "fence" denotes additional boundaries beyond the core prohibition, separating oneself from all its perimeter;
כְּגָדֵר שֶׁעוֹשִׂין לַכֶּרֶם חוּץ לָאִילָנוֹת שֶׁלֹּא יִקְרַב זָר לְתוֹכָם
like a fence built outside the trees of a vineyard to prevent strangers from entering;
וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּחֻלִּין (ק״י עַמּוּד א׳): ״בִּקְעָה מָצָא וְגָדַר בָּהּ גָּדֵר״
as stated in Chullin (110a): "he found an open breach and erected a fence";
בִּבְרָכוֹת (כ״ב סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳): ״גֶּדֶר גָּדוֹל גָּדְרוּ בָּהּ״
in Berachos (22a): "a great fence did they erect therein";
בְּשַׁבָּת (ט״ז עַמּוּד ב׳): ״גֶּדֶר מֵי חַטָּאת״, וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה דּוּכְתֵּי
in Shabbat (16b): "a fence around the water of purification," and in numerous passages;
וְאֵין נִקְרָא ״קָדוֹשׁ״ וְנִמְצָא קְדוּשָׁה אֶלָּא מִי שֶׁמּוֹסִיף לוֹ גְּדָרִים שֶׁלֹּא יָבוֹא לְאִיסּוּר עֶרְוָה, נוֹסָפוֹת עַל גּוּף הָאִיסּוּר שֶׁאֲסָרַתּוּ תּוֹרָה:
and no one is called "holy" save he who erects additional fences so as not to approach immorality, adding beyond the biblical prohibition!
אֲבָל יִשּׁוּב דִּבְרֵי רַשִׁ״י נִרְאֶה עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ לְרָבָא בִּיבָמוֹת שָׁם (כ׳ עַמּוּד א׳) בַּמַּסְקָנָא בִּדְרַבָּנַן
But the reconciliation of Rashi's words appears after the manner the Gemara concluded to Rava in Yevamos (20a) regarding rabbinic law;
הָכִי נַמֵּי בְּשֶׁל תּוֹרָה: מִצַּד תְּחִלַּת הָאַזְהָרָה שֶׁמִּצַּד הַמַּזְהִיר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
so too regarding the Torah itself: from the perspective of the initial command given by Hashem;
שֶׁהָיָה הַדָּבָר מוּתָּר וְהוּא בָּא לְאָסְרָהּ עָלֵינוּ, הוּא בָּא לְקַדְּשֵׁנוּ בַּמֻּתָּר לָנוּ
when the matter was previously permitted and He prohibited it, He came to sanctify us in that which was permitted;
וְכַוָּונָתוֹ הָיָה שֶׁנִּהְיֶה עַל יְדֵי זֶה קְדוֹשִׁים
His intention being that through this we become consecrated.
וְנֶגֶד כְּלַל הָאוּמּוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם, נִקְרְאוּ כְּלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל כּוּלָּם שֶׁקִּבְּלוּ הַתּוֹרָה ״קְדוֹשִׁים״
And relative to all the heathen nations of the world, collective Israel who received the Torah are called "holy";
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״קֹדֶשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל לַה׳, רֵאשִׁית תְּבוּאָתֹה, כָּל אֹכְלָיו יֶאְשָׁמוּ״ (יִרְמְיָה ב:ג)
as it is said: "Israel is holy unto Hashem, the first-fruits of His increase; all that devour him shall be held guilty" (Yirmiyah 2:3);
וּבֵין יִשְׂרָאֵל עַצְמָן, נֶגֶד הָנֵי בִּרְיוֹנֵי הָעַבַרְיָנִים הָעוֹבְרִים עַל דִּבְרֵי חֲכָמִים
and among Israelites themselves, relative to lawless transgressors who violate the words of the Sages;
נִקְרָא הַמְקַיֵּים דִּבְרֵי חֲכָמִים ״קָדוֹשׁ״, וְזֶה טַעַם דְּאַבַּיֵּי
one who observes the words of the Sages is called "holy," this being the reasoning of Abaye;
אֶלָּא דְּלָא נִיחָא לֵיהּ לְרָבָא לְהַעֲמִיד כֵּן לְשׁוֹן הַמִּשְׁנָה, דְּלֹא דִּבְּרוּ מִפְּרִיצִים הָעוֹבְרִים עַל דִּבְרֵי חֲכָמִים
except that Rava was unwilling to interpret the Mishnah thus, the Mishnah not addressing lawless rebels.
וּבֵין כְּשֵׁרֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, נִקְרָא ״קָדוֹשׁ״ מִי שֶׁגּוֹדֵר עַצְמוֹ עוֹד בַּמֻּתָּר
And among observant, upright Israelites, he who fences himself further in the permitted is called "holy";
וּבֵין הַגּוֹדְרִין עַצְמָן גַּם כֵּן יֵשׁ מִי שֶׁנִּקְרָא ״קָדוֹשׁ״ בֵּינֵיהֶם
and among those who practice self-restraint there is likewise one who is singled out as "holy" among them;
כְּשֶׁהוּא גּוֹדֵר עַצְמוֹ בְּיֶתֶר שְׂאֵת, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כָּל הַגּוֹדְרִין גּוֹדְרִים עַצְמָן
when he fences himself with greater elevation beyond what other ascetics observe;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאֱלִישָׁע נִקְרָא ״אִישׁ קָדוֹשׁ״ בְּדוֹרָן שֶׁל נְבִיאִים
just as Elisha was designated a "holy man" in the generation of prophets;
וְרַבֵּינוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ [רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הַנָּשִׂיא] בֵּין הַתַּנָּאִים
and our holy Master [Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi] among the Tannaim;
וּמְפוֹרָשׁ בְּשַׁבָּת (קי״ח עַמּוּד ב׳): דְּשׁוּם תַּנָּא לֹא הָיָה לוֹ הַמַּעֲלָה וְהַגְדָּרַת הַקְּדוּשָׁה בִּשְׁמִירַת הַבְּרִית שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ
and it is explicit in Shabbat (118b): no other Tanna possessed that supreme level of fence in preserving the covenant as Rebbe possessed;
דְּאִם כֵּן הָיָה נִקְרָא גַּם הוּא ״קָדוֹשׁ״, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם
for had another possessed it, he too would have been crowned "holy," see there.
וּבְיָמָיו דְּרַבִּי הָיָה ״קְהִלָּא קַדִּישָׁא דִּבִירוּשָׁלַיִם״
And in Rebbe's days there existed the "Holy Congregation of Jerusalem";
שֶׁהָיָה רַבִּי אוֹמֵר שְׁמוּעוֹת מֵהֶם בְּיוֹמָא (ס״ט עַמּוּד ב׳)
from whom Rebbe cited traditions in Yoma (69b);
שֶׁהֵם הָיוּ בְּיָמָיו וּקְשִׁישֵׁי מִינֵיהּ, כִּמְבוֹאָר בְּבֵיצָה (כ״ז עַמּוּד א׳) בְּרַשִׁ״י, עַיֵּין שָׁם
they being his contemporaries and older than he, as explained by Rashi in Beitzah (27a), see there;
כִּי הָיָה בְּאוֹתוֹ הַדּוֹר הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת קְדוּשָׁה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
for in that generation an expansive light of holiness spread throughout Israel;
וּבֵין כְּלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל קְדוֹשִׁים הַצַּדִּיקִים וְהַחֲסִידִים, נִתְיַיחֵד לִקְדוּשָׁה אוֹתוֹ קְהַל קְדוֹשִׁים שֶׁבִּירוּשָׁלַיִם
and among the holy tzaddikim and chassidim of collective Israel, that Holy Congregation of Jerusalem was set apart for unique sanctity;
וְזָכָה רַבִּי לִהְיוֹת ״קָדוֹשׁ״ בֵּין קְדוֹשִׁים הָאֵלֶּה
and Rebbe merited to be crowned "holy" even among those holy sages;
כִּי הַקְּדוּשָׁה הִיא מַדְרֵיגוֹת מַדְרֵיגוֹת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁיֵּשׁ ״קֹדֶשׁ״ וְ״קֹדֶשׁ הַקֳּדָשִׁים״, וְכֵן בַּנְּפָשׁוֹת:
for holiness proceeds in ascending rungs, just as there is the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies, and so it is among human souls!

2.h: יִשְׂרָאֵל קְדוֹשִׁים — פֶּרֶק ב׳ (הֶמְשֵׁךְ), פֶּרֶק ג׳, וּפֶרֶק ד׳ (פְּתִיחָה)
פֶּרֶק ב׳ — אוֹת ה׳ (הֶמְשֵׁךְ) — Chapter 2: Section 5 (Ascending Rungs of Holiness)

The theme: The distinction of Aharon as Holy of Holies, the ascending ladder of holiness up to the Divine, and the future elevation of the righteous above the ministering angels. In the wilderness generation, Aharon was set apart to be consecrated as Holy of Holies (I Divrei HaYamim 23:13); for although the entire congregation was holy as Korach claimed (Bamidbar 16:3), there exists a holy one among the holy, and whom Hashem chooses is the holiest in such an assembly. These rungs ascend unto the ultimate pinnacle of holiness—the holiness of Hashem Himself—which transcends mortal capacity ("can you be like Me? Scripture states: 'for I am holy'—My holiness is above your holiness", Vayikra Rabbah 24:9). Angels are also consummately holy because they possess no yetzer hara or bodily lust; yet mortals can achieve their level and surpass them. In the Future, the righteous will dwell within a more intimate partition than the ministering angels (Yerushalmi Shabbat 6:9), when the yetzer hara is slaughtered from mankind (Sukkah 52a). Then "he that is left in Zion, and he that remains in Jerusalem, shall be called holy" (Yeshayah 4:3)—the word ye'amer ("shall be called") meaning that others will proclaim him holy, namely the ministering angels, for Israel will be unique in the world ("Hashem alone did lead him", Devarim 32:12), their sanctity surpassing the angels who will gaze upon them in reverence!

p: וּבְדוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר נִבְדַּל אַהֲרֹן ״לְהַקְדִּישׁוֹ קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים״ (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א כ״ג:י״ג)
And in the generation of the wilderness Aharon was separated "to sanctify him as most holy" (I Divrei HaYamim 23:13);
דְּאַף שֶׁכָּל הָעֵדָה הָיוּ כּוּלָּם קְדוֹשִׁים כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר קֹרַח (בַּמִּדְבָּר ט״ז:ג׳)
for even though the entire congregation were all holy as Korach stated (Bamidbar 16:3);
מִכָּל מָקוֹם יֵשׁ קָדוֹשׁ בֵּין קְדוֹשִׁים גַּם כֵּן
nevertheless there exists one who is holy among holy ones as well;
וַאֲשֶׁר יִבְחַר בּוֹ ה׳ הוּא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בֵּין עֵדָה כָּזוֹ שֶׁכּוּלָּם קְדוֹשִׁים
and whom Hashem chooses is the holy one within such an assembly where all are holy.
וְכֵן הוֹלְכִים הַמַּדְרֵיגוֹת עַד תַּכְלִית הַקְּדוּשָׁה, שֶׁהוּא קְדֻשָּׁתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מִקְּדֻשָּׁתֵנוּ, שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לִהְיוֹת כָּמוֹהוּ
And so ascend the rungs unto the ultimate summit of holiness, which is the sanctity of the Blessed One transcending our holiness, it being impossible to be like Him;
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה כ״ד:ט׳)
as the Sages stated in Vayikra Rabbah (24:9) [on "You shall be holy, for I am holy"—My holiness is superior to yours].
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הַמַּלְאָכִים, אַף שֶׁהֵם גַּם כֵּן קְדוֹשִׁים בְּתַכְלִית, שֶׁהֲרֵי אֵין בָּהֶם יֵצֶר הָרָע וְתַאֲוָה כְּלָל
Unlike the angels, who although they are likewise consummately holy, having no evil inclination or physical lust whatsoever;
מִכָּל מָקוֹם אֶפְשָׁר לִבְנֵי אָדָם לִהְיוֹת כְּמוֹהֶם
nevertheless it is possible for human beings to attain their stature.
וְלֶעָתִיד יִהְיוּ צַדִּיקִים לִפְנִים מִמַּלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי (סוֹף פֶּרֶק ו׳ דְּשַׁבָּת הֲלָכָה ט׳)
And in the Future the righteous will dwell within a more interior partition than the ministering angels, as stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Shabbat 6:9);
וְהַיְינוּ כְּשֶׁיִּתְבַּטֵּל הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע גַּם מִבְּנֵי אָדָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (נ״ב עַמּוּד א׳)
meaning when the evil inclination is abolished from mankind as well, as stated in Sukkah (52a);
וְאָז: ״[וְהָיָה] כָּל הַנִּשְׁאָר בְּצִיּוֹן [וְהַנּוֹתָר בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם] — קָדוֹשׁ יֵאָמֶר לוֹ״ (יְשַׁעְיָה ד:ג)
and then: "he that is left in Zion, and he that remains in Jerusalem, shall be called holy" (Yeshayah 4:3).
וְהַךְ ״יֵאָמֵר״ — דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁאֲחֵרִים יֹאמְרוּ כֵּן, הַיְינוּ מַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת
And this word "shall be called" (ye'amer) means that others will proclaim him so, namely the ministering angels;
כִּי אָז יִהְיוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לְבַד בָּעוֹלָם, דְּ״ה׳ בָּדָד יַנְחֶנּוּ [וְאֵין עִמּוֹ אֵל נֵכָר]״ (דְּבָרִים ל״ב:י״ב)
for then the Children of Israel will dwell alone in the world: "Hashem alone did lead him, and there was no strange god with him" (Devarim 32:12);
וּקְדֻשָּׁתָם יִהְיֶה לְמַעְלָה מִקְּדֻשַּׁת הַמַּלְאָכִים
and their holiness will transcend the holiness of the angels;
עַד שֶׁמִּי שֶׁנֶּחְשָׁב לַנִּשְׁאָר וְנוֹתָר בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם יֹאמְרוּ הֵם לוֹ ״קָדוֹשׁ״
to the extent that even one considered merely a common remnant in Jerusalem, the angels will proclaim him "holy";
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נִקְרָא בֵּינֵיהֶם בְּשֵׁם ״קָדוֹשׁ״ סְתָם כְּפִי עֵרֶךְ קְדֻשָּׁתוֹ נֶגְדָּם
he being designated among them as "holy" unconditionally relative to their own stature.
וּמִזֶּה נֵדַע כַּמָּה מַדְרֵיגוֹת יֵשׁ בַּקְּדוּשָׁה
And from this we may know how many ascending rungs exist within holiness;
וְרַק לִהְיוֹת כָּמוֹהוּ כִּבְיָכוֹל — זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר:
and only to be like Him, as it were, is impossible!

3.h: פֶּרֶק ג׳ — אוֹת א׳ (פְּרִישׁוּת וּקְדוּשָׁה בַּמִּקְרָא וּבַחֲזַ״ל) — Chapter 3: Section 1 (Abstinence and Holiness in Scripture and Chazal)

The theme: Sanctifying oneself in the permitted, the Ramban's doctrine against the Torah scoundrel, and the distinction between Perishut and Kedushah. What is the nature of sanctification in the permitted? Torat Kohanim teaches on "You shall be holy" (Vayikra 19:2): "Be abstinent (perushim)". The Ramban expounds that this is an independent commandment to separate from superfluities, guarding against becoming a "scoundrel with the Torah's permission" (naval bi-rshut ha-Torah), such as scholars being intimate with their wives like roosters (Berachos 22a). A Nazirite is called holy on account of his abstinence from wine (Bamidbar 6:5; Maharsha on Yevamos 20a). Vayikra Rabbah (24:4) states: "Just as I am abstinent, so shall you be abstinent; just as I am holy, so shall you be holy". In Avodah Zarah (20b), Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair lists abstinence (perishut) and holiness (kedushah) as two separate stages, Rashi explaining that abstinence means refraining from permitted things to be stringent upon oneself, while holiness is an even higher rung. In Sotah (20a, 22b), the Sages discuss the hypocritical "abstinent woman" and the seven classes of false ascetics who act like Zimri and seek the reward of Pinchas, demonstrating that abstinence centers primarily upon sexual desires. In Scripture, abstinence is subsumed within holiness as its initial lower stage, whereas the Talmud delineates them into two distinct rungs.

p: וּמַהוּ הַקִּידּוּשׁ בַּמֻּתָּר?
And what is the nature of sanctification in that which is permitted?
אָמְרוּ בְּתוֹרַת כֹּהֲנִים (רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת קְדוֹשִׁים): ״׳קְדֹשִׁים תִּהְיוּ׳ — פְּרוּשִׁים תִּהְיוּ״
The Sages stated in Torat Kohanim (beginning of Parashat Kedoshim): "'You shall be holy'—you shall be abstinent (perushim)";
וּפֵירֵשׁ הָרַמְבַּ״ן עַל הַתּוֹרָה שָׁם: דְּהוּא מִצְוָה בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ לִפְרוֹשׁ מִן הַמּוֹתָרוֹת
and the Ramban on the Torah expounded there: that this is an independent commandment to separate from physical superfluities;
וְשֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה ״נָבָל בִּרְשׁוּת הַתּוֹרָה״
and that one should not become a "scoundrel with the permission of the Torah";
וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת כ״ב עַמּוּד א׳): שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים מְצוּיִין אֵצֶל נְשׁוֹתֵיהֶם כְּתַרְנְגוֹלִים
after the manner stated in Berachos (22a): that Torah scholars should not frequent their wives like roosters;
וְכֵן בִּשְׁאָר עִנְיָנִים, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם בַּאֲרִיכוּת
and so regarding all other bodily appetites, see there at length.
וְהֵבִיא רְאָיָה מִנָּזִיר שֶׁנִּקְרָא ״קָדוֹשׁ״ עַל שֵׁם פְּרִישׁוּתוֹ
And the Ramban brought proof from the Nazirite who is designated "holy" on account of his abstinence from wine;
וְכֵן כָּתַב רְאָיָה זוֹ הַמַּהַרְשָׁ״א בְּחִדּוּשֵׁי אַגָּדוֹת (יְבָמוֹת כ׳ עַמּוּד א׳), עַיֵּין שָׁם
and so wrote this proof the Maharsha in his Chiddushei Aggadot (Yevamos 20a), see there;
וּבְוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה כ״ד:ד׳) אִיתָא: ״כְּשֵׁם שֶׁאֲנִי פָּרוּשׁ כָּךְ תִּהְיוּ פְּרוּשִׁים, כְּשֵׁם שֶׁאֲנִי קָדוֹשׁ כָּךְ תִּהְיוּ קְדוֹשִׁים, הֲדָא הוּא דִכְתִיב: ׳קְדֹשִׁים תִּהְיוּ׳״
and in Vayikra Rabbah (24:4) it is taught: "Just as I am abstinent so shall you be abstinent, just as I am holy so shall you be holy; that is what is written: 'You shall be holy'";
וְכִלְשׁוֹן זֶה גַּם כֵּן בְּתוֹרַת כֹּהֲנִים (סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת קְדוֹשִׁים) עַל פָּסוּק: ״וִהְיִיתֶם לִי קְדֹשִׁים [כִּי קָדוֹשׁ אֲנִי ה׳]״ (וַיִּקְרָא כ:כו)
and similarly phrased in Torat Kohanim (end of Parashat Kedoshim) on the verse: "And you shall be holy unto Me, for I Hashem am holy" (Vayikra 20:26).
וְהִנֵּה דְּחָשֵׁיב בִּתְרַתֵּי: ״פְּרוּשִׁים״ וּ״קְדוֹשִׁים״
And behold, Scripture enumerates two distinct qualities: "abstinent" and "holy";
אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם כַּיְלִינְהוּ תַּרְוַויְיהוּ בִּ״קְדֹשִׁים״ דִּקְרָא
yet Scripture encompasses both within the single term "holy";
וְגַם בְּסֵדֶר הַמַּדְרֵיגוֹת בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (כ׳ עַמּוּד ב׳) חָשֵׁיב ״פְּרִישׁוּת״ וּ״קְדוּשָׁה״ בִּתְרַתֵּי
and also in the ladder of rungs in Avodah Zarah (20b), Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair counts abstinence and holiness as two separate rungs;
וּפֵירֵשׁ רַשִׁ״י: ״פְּרִישׁוּת — אַף מִדָּבָר הַמֻּתָּר פּוֹרֵשׁ לְהַחְמִיר עַל עַצְמוֹ״
and Rashi explained: "abstinence—even from a permitted thing one separates to be stringent upon himself";
וּמַשְׁמַע דִּ״קְדוּשָׁה״ הוּא עִנְיָן אַחֵר לְמַעְלָה מִזֶּה
implying that holiness is a distinct, more exalted stage above this.
וּפֵירוּשׁ ״פְּרִישׁוּת״ בְּכָל מָקוֹם הוּא כֵּן: לִפְרוֹשׁ מִכָּל מִינֵי תַּאֲווֹת כְּמַשְׁמָעוֹ שֶׁל מִלַּת ״פָּרוּשׁ״
And the definition of "abstinence" everywhere is thus: to separate from all physical desires, as the literal meaning of the word parush;
וּבְסוֹטָה (כ׳ עַמּוּד א׳): ״אִשָּׁה פְּרוּשָׁה וּמַכַּת פְּרוּשִׁין״
and in Sotah (20a): "a hypocritical abstinent woman and the plagues of the Pharisees";
עַיֵּין שָׁם בַּגְּמָרָא (כ״ב עַמּוּד א׳) וּבְרַשִׁ״י עַל ״אִשָּׁה״
see the Gemara there (22a) and Rashi regarding this woman;
וְשָׁם (עַמּוּד ב׳): ״שִׁבְעָה פְּרוּשִׁין הֵן וְכוּלֵיהּ... עַד שֶׁעוֹשִׂים מַעֲשֵׂה זִמְרִי [וּמְבַקְּשִׁין שָׂכָר כְּפִינְחָס]״
and there (22b): "there are seven classes of Pharisees... who commit the licentious deed of Zimri and seek the reward of Pinchas";
שֶׁבָּזֶה הוּא עִיקַּר הַפְּרִישׁוּת
for in sexual restraint lies the primary arena of abstinence.
וּבִלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב גַּם זֶה בִּכְלַל ״קְדוּשָׁה״
And in the language of Scripture this bodily restraint is likewise included in the term "holiness";
דְּזֶהוּ אַתְחַלְתָּא דִּקְדוּשָׁה: מַה שֶּׁאָדָם מְקַדֵּשׁ עַצְמוֹ מִלְּמַטָּה הוּא עַל יְדֵי שֶׁפּוֹרֵשׁ מִתַּאֲווֹתָיו הַמֻּתָּרוֹת
for this is the inception of holiness: man sanctifying himself below by separating from permissible bodily pleasures;
אֲבָל בִּלְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים בְּתַלְמוּדָא דִּידַן חֲלוּקִין לִשְׁנַיִם:
whereas in the precise terminology of the Sages in our Babylonian Talmud, they are divided into two distinct stages!

3.h: פֶּרֶק ג׳ — אוֹת ב׳ (גִּרְסַת הַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי וְהַבַּבְלִי בְּסֻלַּם רַבִּי פִּנְחָס בֶּן יָאִיר) — Chapter 3: Section 2 (The Textual Variations in the Ladder of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair)

The theme: The variants between the Bavli and Yerushalmi in Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's ladder, and the Sephardic versus Ashkenazic textual traditions. In Yerushalmi Shabbat (1:3) and Shekalim (3:3), the ladder of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair omits perishut (abstinence) and places kedushah (holiness) where our Talmud places abstinence, citing "and they were cleansed and they were sanctified" (Divrei HaYamim), placing chasidut (piety) at the end. The Maharsha and Mahari Bei Rav preferred this version; yet the Rosh established that Ashkenazic textual traditions are inherited master to student and are deeply authoritative, warning against emending our Talmud based on Spanish texts. The Babylonian Talmud’s version is exact: the Yerushalmi placed kedushah earlier to denote the inception of holiness—which is the physical abstinence from permitted pleasures that is within human strength to control. The kedushah placed at the very summit of our Babylonian Talmud is an entirely different, transcendent divine gift. The Yerushalmi calls this ultimate stage chasidut (piety), not meaning ordinary piety (performing extra stringencies in action), but the supreme piety granted when Hashem places His Spirit within man ("and I will put My Spirit within you", Yechezkel 36:27; Ran on Avodah Zarah), which is the consummation of supernal holiness bestowed from Above.

p: וּבַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי פֶּרֶק א׳ דְּשַׁבָּת (סוֹף הֲלָכָה ג׳) וְסוֹף פֶּרֶק ג׳ דִּשְׁקָלִים (הֲלָכָה ג׳) אִיתָא גַּם כֵּן הָנֵי מַדְרֵיגוֹת דְּרַבִּי פִּנְחָס בֶּן יָאִיר, וְלֹא חָשֵׁיב שָׁם ״פְּרִישׁוּת״
And in the Jerusalem Talmud (Shabbat 1:3 and Shekalim 3:3) these rungs of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair are likewise recorded, but abstinence (perishut) is not enumerated there;
וְכֵן הוּא גַּם בְּרֵישׁ שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים [רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה א:א]
and so it is found at the beginning of Shir HaShirim Rabbah (1:1);
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם הַסֵּדֶר: ״קְדוּשָׁה״ בִּמְקוֹם ״פְּרִישׁוּת״ דְּתַלְמוּדָא דִּידַן, וּמַיְיתֵי קְרָא דְּ״טָהֲרוּ וְקָדְשׁוּ״, וְ״חֲסִידוּת״ הוּא הָאַחֲרוֹנָה שָׁם
and see the sequence there: "holiness" occupies the place of "abstinence" in our Talmud, citing the verse "and they were cleansed and they were sanctified," with "piety" listed as the final rung;
וְהַמַּהַרְשָׁ״א בְּחִדּוּשֵׁי אַגָּדוֹת שָׁם תָּפַס נוּסְחָא זוֹ עִיקָּר, עַיֵּין שָׁם
and the Maharsha in his Chiddushei Aggadot adopted that version as primary, see there;
וְגַם מַהֲרִי״ב [רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב בֵּירַב] בְּגִלְיוֹן הַגְּמָרָא הִגִּיהַּ שָׁם נוּסְחַת תַּלְמוּדָא דִּידַן
and the Mahari Bei Rav in the margins of the Gemara likewise emended our talmudic text.

וֶאֱמֶת מִדִּבְרֵי רַשִׁ״י (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כ׳ סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳ דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל: ״אָז דִּבַּרְתָּ״) שֶׁכָּתַב: ״וְלֹא נֶאֱמַר לִירֵאֶיךָ וְלַעֲנָוֶיךָ״, וְלֹא אָמַר טְפֵי ״לִקְדוֹשֶׁיךָ״, מַשְׁמַע גַּם כֵּן קְצָת כֵּן

And in truth from the words of Rashi in Avodah Zarah (20b, s.v. Az dibarta), noting that the verse does not say "to Your reverent ones or humble ones," and not mentioning "to Your holy ones," it implies somewhat like that reading;
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין בָּזֶה הַכְרֵעַ כָּל כָּךְ
nevertheless there is no decisive proof in this.
וּכְבָר נוֹדַע דִּבְרֵי הַקַּדְמוֹנִים שֶׁאֵין לְהַגִּיהַּ הַסְּפָרִים בְּקַל כָּל כָּךְ
And the warning of early authorities is well known: that one must not emend sacred texts lightly;

וְהֲגַם דְּמָצָא כֵן בְּ״עֵין יַעֲקֹב״ וְרִי״ף, נוֹדַע כַּמָּה שִׁינּוּיִים יֵשׁ בְּכַמָּה דּוּכְתֵּי בֵּין נוּסְחָאוֹתֵיהֶם שֶׁהֵם נוּסְחַת סְפָרַדִּית לְנוּסְחַת תַּלְמוּדָא דִּידַן שֶׁהוּא נוּסְחַת אַשְׁכְּנַזִּית וְצָרְפַתִּית
and although he found this reading in the Ein Yaakov and the Rif, it is recognized that their Spanish texts differ in numerous places from our Ashkenazic and French talmudic traditions;
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָרַמְבַּ״ן שֶׁהָיָה מִבְּנֵי סְפָרַד מִשְׁתַּבֵּחַ תָּמִיד בַּנּוּסְחָאוֹת הַסְּפָרַדִּיּוֹת בְּ״מִלְחֲמוֹת ה׳״ וּבְחִדּוּשָׁיו
and even though the Ramban praised the Spanish versions in Milchamot Hashem and his commentaries;
הָרֹא״שׁ שֶׁהָיָה מִצֶּאֱצָאֵי אַשְׁכְּנַז כָּתַב בִּתְשׁוּבוֹת: דִּלִבְנֵי אַשְׁכְּנַז הַתּוֹרָה יְרוּשָׁה מִדּוֹר דּוֹר, וְקַבָּלָתָם עֲדִיפָא מִקַּבָּלַת בְּנֵי סְפָרַד

the Rosh, originating from Ashkenaz, wrote in his Responsa: unto the scholars of Ashkenaz the Torah is an unbroken heritage from generation to generation, and their tradition is superior to that of Spain;
וּמַה גַּם בְּנוּסְחַת הַתַּלְמוּד, אֵין לְהַזְנִיחַ נוּסְחָא הַמְקוּבֶּלֶת בְּיָדֵינוּ מֵאֲבוֹתֵינוּ
and especially regarding the text of the Talmud, one must never abandon the received tradition handed down from our fathers;
וְגַם מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב מַהֲרִי״ב מִסּוֹטָה, אַף הוּא אֵינֶנָּה בְּנוּסְחָאוֹתֵינוּ כָּל עִיקָּר שָׁם, וּבְוַדַּאי גַּם הוּא נוּסְחָא סְפָרַדִּית
and what the Mahari Bei Rav cited from Sotah does not exist in our versions, being likewise a Spanish manuscript.
וּלְדַעְתִּי נוּסְחָתֵנוּ בְּכָאן אֶפְשָׁר לְקַיְּימָהּ שַׁפִּיר
And in my humble opinion our received text can be beautifully upheld:
וְהַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי שֶׁהִקְדִּים ״קְדוּשָׁה״, כַּוָּונָתוֹ לְאַתְחַלְתָּא דִּקְדוּשָׁה, וְהוּא הַ״פְּרִישׁוּת״ שֶׁבְּתַלְמוּדָא דִּידַן בִּמְקוֹמָהּ
the Jerusalem Talmud which placed "holiness" earlier referred to the inception of holiness, which corresponds exactly to "abstinence" in our Babylonian Talmud;
וְדָבָר זֶה אֵין כָּבֵד כָּל כָּךְ עַל הַגּוּף, שֶׁבְּיַד הָאָדָם לִשְׁלוֹט עַל יִצְרוֹ וְלִבְלוֹם תַּאֲווֹתָיו כִּרְצוֹנוֹ
this discipline not weighing so heavily upon the body, it being within human control to restrain bodily desires;
אֲבָל הַקְּדוּשָׁה שֶׁבְּתַלְמוּדָא דִּידַן הַשְּׁנוּיָה בָּאַחֲרוֹנָה, שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לָבוֹא לָהּ אֶלָּא בְּסוֹף כָּל הַמַּדְרֵיגוֹת — הוּא עִנְיָן אַחֵר
but the holiness recorded at the end of our Babylonian Talmud, which cannot be attained except following all rungs, is an entirely different matter.
וְנִרְאֶה לִי דְּהַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי קָרֵי לָזוֹ ״חֲסִידוּת״
And it appears to me that the Jerusalem Talmud designates this ultimate level "piety" (chasidut);
דְּאֵין כַּוָּונָתוֹ בָּהּ לַחֲסִידוּת דְּתַלְמוּדָא דִּידַן, שֶׁהַכַּוָּונָה בוֹ לַחֲסִידוּת הַמּוּרְגָּל בְּכָל מָקוֹם, דְּרָצָה לוֹמַר: הַמַּחְמִיר עַל עַצְמוֹ בְּדָבָר הַמֻּתָּר עַל פִּי הַדִּין
not referring to ordinary piety, which means voluntarily adopting extra stringencies beyond the strict law;
וְהִנֵּה זֶה כְּמוֹ הַפְּרִישׁוּת מִן הַמֻּתָּר, אֶלָּא שֶׁזֶּה רַק בְּעִנְיְנֵי תַּאֲווֹת וּבְ״שֵׁב וְאַל תַּעֲשֶׂה״, וְהַחֲסִידוּת בְּכָל עִנְיָנִים וּבְ״קוּם וַעֲשֵׂה״ גַּם כֵּן
that being like abstinence in passive restraint, whereas ordinary piety operates actively across all realms;
וְהַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי כָּיֵיל תַּרְוַויְיהוּ בִּ״קְדוּשָׁה״ שֶׁהוּא לְקַדֵּשׁ עַצְמוֹ לִפְרוֹשׁ וּלְהַחְמִיר עַל עַצְמוֹ בְּדָבָר הַמֻּתָּר, וְהַחֲסִידוּת שָׁנָה בָּאַחֲרוֹנָה
the Yerushalmi combining both under the earlier stage of "holiness," placing this transcendent piety at the end.
וּכְפִי הַגִּרְסָא בְּשַׁבָּת וְכֵן הוּא בָּרִי״ף בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה: ״חֲסִידוּת אַחַר רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ״
And according to the text in Shabbat and the Rif in Avodah Zarah: "piety follows the Holy Spirit";
עַל כָּרְחָךְ: ״וְנָתַתִּי רוּחִי בָּכֶם״ (יְחֶזְקֵאל ל״ו:כ״ז) הַיְינוּ חֲסִידוּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַ״ן שָׁם
perforce "and I will put My Spirit within you" (Yechezkel 36:27) denotes this supreme piety, as the Ran writes there;
צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר דְּדָבָר זֶה אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי מַה שֶּׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נוֹתֵן רוּחוֹ בּוֹ
one must conclude that this stage is attained solely through the Holy One placing His Spirit within man;
וְזֶהוּ עַצְמוֹ שְׁלֵימוּת הַקְּדוּשָׁה מַה שֶּׁמְּקַדְּשִׁין אוֹתוֹ מִלְּמַעְלָה:
this being the consummation of holiness: when man is consecrated from Above!
פֶּרֶק ג׳ — אוֹת ג׳ (הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת הָאָדָם וְסִיַּעְתָּא דִּשְׁמַיָּא) — Chapter 3: Section 3 (Human Striving and Divine Assistance)

The theme: The Babylonian Talmud listing human acquisitions, and David HaMelech attaining a slain yetzer hara. Our Babylonian Talmud enumerates strictly those spiritual rungs that lie within human power to achieve through personal striving. That which Hashem bestows as an unearned gift is consummate piety (chasidut), granted unto masters of the Holy Spirit. King David—the master of the Holy Spirit—referred to himself as a "chassid" (Berachos 4a), meriting that his heart became an empty void within him (libi chalal b'kirbi, Tehillim 109:22), the yetzer hara having no dominion over him (Avodah Zarah 4b; Sukkah 52a). This victory is impossible without divine assistance: "the yetzer hara renews itself daily against man, and were it not for Hashem's help he could not overcome it" (Sukkah 52a; Yoma 38b). Hashem assists only he who comes to purify himself ("He will keep the feet of His pious ones", I Shmuel 2:9). When a person exerts himself to the utmost limit of human capacity in abstinence and piety, Hashem sends help from the Sanctuary, placing His Spirit within him: "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh" (Yechezkel 36:26).
וְתַלְמוּדָא דִּידַן חָשֵׁיב רַק הַמַּדְרֵיגוֹת שֶׁבְּיַד הָאָדָם לְהַשִּׂיג בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ
And our Babylonian Talmud enumerates strictly those rungs within man's power to attain through his own striving;
וְזֶה מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נוֹתֵן הוּא שְׁלֵימוּת הַחֲסִידוּת הַגְּדוֹלָה מִכּוּלָּן, שֶׁזּוֹכִין לָהּ בַּעֲלֵי רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ
and that which the Blessed Name bestows as a gift is the perfection of piety—the greatest of all—merited by masters of the Holy Spirit;
וּכְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם רַבָּן שֶׁל בַּעֲלֵי רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ, דְּקָרֵי לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ ״חָסִיד״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (ד׳ עַמּוּד א׳)
like King David, the master of those who possess the Holy Spirit, who called himself a chassid (Berachos 4a);
זָכָה לִהְיוֹת ״לִבִּי חָלָל בְּקִרְבִּי״ (תְּהִלִּים ק״ט:כ״ב), שֶׁלֹּא שָׁלַט בּוֹ יֵצֶר הָרָע, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (ד׳ סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳)
meriting that his heart was slain within him (Tehillim 109:22), the yetzer hara having no dominion over him (Avodah Zarah 4b).
וְדָבָר זֶה אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזְרוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (נ״ב רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳)
And this total victory occurs solely through the Holy One assisting him, as stated in Sukkah (52b);
אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזֵר אֶלָּא לְמִי שֶׁ״בָּא לִטָּהֵר״, דְּהַמִּשְׁפָּט לִהְיוֹת ״מְסַיְּיעִין אוֹתוֹ״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (ל״ח סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳)
but the Holy One assists only him who comes to purify himself, the divine rule being to support him (Yoma 38b);
וּמַיְיתֵי שָׁם לִפְנֵי זֶה הָא דִּ״רַגְלֵי חֲסִידָו יִשְׁמֹר״ (שְׁמוּאֵל א ב:ט)
citing there the verse: "He will keep the feet of His pious ones" (I Shmuel 2:9);
דְּצָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּשְׁתַּדֵּל בִּפְרִישׁוּת וַחֲסִידוּת בְּדָבָר הַמֻּתָּר כְּדֵי לִזְכּוֹת לִשְׁמִירָה וְסִיּוּעַ שֶׁמִּלְּמַעְלָה
that one must exert himself in abstinence and piety in the permitted in order to merit protection and assistance from Above;
בַּמַּה שֶּׁהוּא אֵין יָכוֹל לְהֵעָזֵר מֵעַצְמוֹ גַּם אַחַר כָּל הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ בִּפְרִישׁוּת וַחֲסִידוּת הָאֶפְשָׁר
in those deep bodily instincts where he cannot help himself even after all humanly possible striving;
אָז הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹלֵחַ עֶזְרוֹ מִקֹּדֶשׁ, מִקִּידּוּשׁ מַעֲשִׂים שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ, וְאֶת רוּחוֹ יִתֵּן בְּקִרְבּוֹ דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה הוּא הָעֵזֶר
then Hashem sends help from the Sanctuary in response to the sanctification of his deeds, placing His Spirit within him;
כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (יְחֶזְקֵאל י״א:י״ט): ״וְרוּחַ חֲדָשָׁה אֶתֵּן בְּקִרְבְּכֶם, וַהֲסִרֹתִי לֵב הָאֶבֶן [מִבְּשָׂרָם, וְנָתַתִּי לָהֶם לֵב בָּשָׂר]״
as it is said: "and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them a heart of flesh" (Yechezkel 11:19);
וְתַלְמוּדָא דִּידַן לֹא חָשֵׁיב מַה שֶּׁאֵינוֹ מֵהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ אֶלָּא ״רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ״:
and our Babylonian Talmud lists among the stages that transcend mortal effort only "the Holy Spirit"!
פֶּרֶק ד׳ — אוֹת א׳ (פְּתִיחָה: כָּל מַעֲשָׂיו לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וְעוֹנַת תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים) — Chapter 4: Section 1 (All Deeds for Heaven, and the Conjugal Onah of Scholars)

The theme: Acting entirely for the sake of Heaven, the Torah as a spice (tavlin), and the marital conduct of King David. The holiness mentioned at the summit of our Babylonian Talmud corresponds to the supreme piety of the Jerusalem Talmud, which the Ran interprets as: "all his deeds are purely for the sake of Heaven". In Kiddushin (81b), the Sages state that where one acts purely for the sake of Heaven, rigid fences regarding proximity to women are suspended (such as Rav Acha holding a bride upon his shoulders, or a grandfather embracing his granddaughter). When a person acts purely for Heaven, he does not require defensive abstinence from permitted physical pleasures, for the Torah acts as an antidote (tavlin, Kiddushin 30b)—spicing the physical food and transforming bodily pleasures (eating, drinking, and washing) into elevated spiritual service. The Or Zarua cites Berachos (22a) that scholars should not frequent their wives like roosters, their marital visitation (onah) being Friday night (Kesubos 62b); yet the Talmud relates that Mar Zutra’s grandson was constantly with his wife (ibid. 62b), which the Or Zarua interprets as twilight (bein ha-shemashot) of every day! Commentators explain bei shimshei as Friday night (see Yerushalmi Bikkurim 3:3; Shitah Mekubetzet citing the students of Rabbeinu Yonah). The Gemara in Sanhedrin (107a) states that King David—the head of all scholars in his generation (Sanhedrin 36a)—cohabited every night even during illness. A king is classified as a gentleman of leisure (taval), whose marital obligation is daily (Kesubos 62a; Beit Shmuel §76). Having eighteen wives, each entitled to her weekly onah, David was engaged every night; yet how does this accord with the warning against acting like roosters, which the Ramban terms becoming a scoundrel with the Torah’s permission?
אֲבָל ״הַקְּדוּשָׁה״ הַמֻּזְכָּר בְּתַלְמוּדָא דִּידַן הוּא ״הַחֲסִידוּת״ דִּירוּשַׁלְמִי
But the "holiness" mentioned in our Babylonian Talmud is identical to the "piety" of the Jerusalem Talmud;
שֶׁפֵּירֵשׁ הָרַ״ן שָׁם: ״דְּכָל מַעֲשָׂיו — לְשֵׁם שָׁמָיִם״
which the Ran explained there: that "all his deeds are solely for the sake of Heaven";
וּבְסוֹף קִדּוּשִׁין (פ״א סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳ — פ״ב רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳) אִיתָא: ״הַכֹּל לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם״
and at the end of Kiddushin (81b–82a) it is taught: "everything depends upon whether it is for the sake of Heaven";
לְעִנְיָן שֶׁאֵין צָרִיךְ כָּל כָּךְ הַגְדָּרָה מֵעֶרְוָה לְעִנְיַן שִׁימּוּשׁ בְּאִשָּׁה, וּמַה דְּנָקַט בַּת בְּרַתֵּיהּ תּוֹתֵי כְּנָפָיו, עַיֵּין שָׁם
regarding not requiring rigid fences from women in domestic proximity, such as holding one's granddaughter under his cloak, see there;
וְהַכַּוָּונָה: דְּמִי שֶׁכָּל מַעֲשָׂיו לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, אֵין צָרִיךְ כָּל כָּךְ פְּרִישׁוּת מִן הַמֻּתָּר שֶׁהוּא רַק מִפַּחַד הַיֵּצֶר
the meaning being: one whose deeds are purely for Heaven does not need defensive abstinence from the permitted, which is instituted solely out of fear of the yetzer.
וְכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (ל׳ עַמּוּד ב׳) לְעִנְיַן: ״תּוֹרָה — תַּבְלִין לַיֵּצֶר״, מָשָׁל לְרוֹפֵא וְכוּלֵיהּ: ״אֱכוֹל וּשְׁתֵה מַה שֶּׁהֲנָאָתְךָ, וּרְחוֹץ וְכוּלֵיהּ״
And so the Sages taught in Kiddushin (30b) regarding "Torah is an antidote (tavlin) to the yetzer," a parable of a physician: "eat and drink whatever gives you pleasure, and wash, etc.";
עַיֵּין שָׁם: דִּכְשֶׁשָּׁמוּר מֵהַיֵּצֶר עַל יְדֵי הַתּוֹרָה, יוּכַל לְהִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בַּהֲנָאוֹתָיו: אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה וּרְחִיצָה וְכַדּוֹמֶה
that when one is protected by the Torah, he can engage in worldly pleasures: eating, drinking, and washing;
וְהַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי שֶׁכָּל כַּוָּונָתוֹ בִּקְדוּשָׁה וּלְשֵׁם שָׁמָיִם
namely because his entire focus is dedicated in holiness for the sake of Heaven;
וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ ״תַּבְלִין״, שֶׁהוּא דָּבָר הַמְתַבֵּל הַמַּאֲכָל, וְעוֹשֶׂה מִשֶּׁאֵינוֹ טוֹב דָּבָר טוֹב וּמְשֻׁבָּח
this being the definition of a "spice" (tavlin), which flavors raw food, transforming an unpalatable substance into a savory, elevated delicacy.
וְעַיֵּין בְּ״אוֹר זָרוּעַ״ גָּדוֹל הַנִּדְפָּס מֵחָדָשׁ חֵלֶק א׳ סוֹף סִימָן ש״ס
And see in the Or Zarua HaGadol (Part I, end of §360);
שֶׁהֵבִיא הָא דִּבְרָכוֹת (כ״ב עַמּוּד א׳): שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים מְצוּיִין וְכוּלֵיהּ, וְעוֹנַת תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים מֵעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת לְעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת (כְּתוּבּוֹת ס״ב עַמּוּד ב׳)
citing Berachos (22a) that scholars should not frequent their wives like roosters, their marital visitation being Friday night (Kesubos 62b);
וְכָתַב: ״מִיהוּ הַהוּא עוּבְדָא וְכוּלֵיהּ, שֶׁאִלְמָלֵא יְהוּדָה קַיָּם לֹא בִּטֵּל עוֹנָתוֹ וְכוּלֵיהּ (שָׁם), מַשְׁמַע דִּמְעַלְּיוּתָא הוּא שֶׁהָיָה תָּדִיר אֵצֶל אִשְׁתּוֹ״, עַד כָּאן

and wrote: "however, the incident of Mar Zutra's grandson (Kesubos 62b)—where had he lived he would not have neglected his onah—implies it was praiseworthy that he was constantly with his wife," thus far;
וּמְפָרֵשׁ ״כָּל בֵּי שִׁמְשֵׁי״ עַל בֵּין הַשְּׁמָשׁוֹת דְּכָל יוֹם
interpreting kol bei shimshei as the twilight of every single day!
וְאוּלַי טַעְמוֹ בָּזֶה מִדְּצִוָּוה לִנְהוֹג אֲבֵילוּת דִּכְפִיַּית הַמִּטָּה וּכְבָר הָיָה בֵּין הַשְּׁמָשׁוֹת, וּבְמוֹעֵד קָטָן (כ״ז עַמּוּד א׳): זְקִיפַת הַמִּטָּה חוֹבָה
And perhaps his reason is because the master commanded to observe mourning by overturning the bed at twilight, while on Shabbat overturning is prohibited (Moed Katan 27a);
וְכָל הַמְפָרְשִׁים מַשְׁמַע דִּמְפָרְשֵׁי ״כְּבֵי שִׁמְשֵׁי״ דְּכָל הַשַּׁ״ס, דְּהַיְינוּ לֵיל שַׁבָּת
yet all other commentators interpret bei shimshei as Friday night;
(וְנִרְאֶה לִי רְאָיָה לְפֵירוּשׁ הַמְפָרְשִׁים מֵהַסִּפּוּר שֶׁבַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי פֶּרֶק ג׳ דְּבִכּוּרִים הֲלָכָה ג׳... דְּאִיתָא שָׁם דְּהָיָה בְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת, עַיֵּין שָׁם)
(and proof for this consensus appears from the narrative in Yerushalmi Bikkurim 3:3 which occurred on Friday evening, see there);
וְכֵן הוּא בְּ״שִׁטָּה מְקֻבֶּצֶת״ שָׁם בִּכְתוּבּוֹת בְּשֵׁם תַּלְמִידֵי רַבֵּינוּ יוֹנָה
and so is recorded in Shitah Mekubetzet in the name of the students of Rabbeinu Yonah.
וְהָעַמּוּדָא דְּנוּרָא שֶׁהָיָה נִרְאֶה קוֹדֶם בִּיאָתוֹ הָיָה מִבְּעוֹד יוֹם, דְּהָיָה עַדַיִין פְּנַאי לִכְפּוֹת וְלִנְהוֹג אֲבֵילוּת שָׁעָה קַלָּה
And the pillar of fire seen prior to his arrival appeared while it was yet day, leaving time to overturn the bed and observe mourning briefly;
וַהֲוָה לֵיהּ לְהָבִיא מִסַּנְהֶדְרִין (ק״ז עַמּוּד א׳): ״אֲפִילּוּ בִּשְׁעַת חָלְיוֹ... בְּכָל לַיְלָה וְכוּלֵיהּ״
and the Or Zarua should rather have brought proof from Sanhedrin (107a): that even during his illness King David cohabited every single night;
וְכִלּוּם יֵשׁ תַּלְמִיד חָכָם יוֹתֵר מִדָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהָיָה רֹאשׁ הַתַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּדוֹרוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם (ל״ו עַמּוּד א׳) וּבְכַמָּה דּוּכְתֵּי
and is there any scholar greater than King David, who was the head of all scholars in his generation (Sanhedrin 36a);
וְלִכְאוֹרָה מִשּׁוּם דְּמֶלֶךְ יֵשׁ לוֹ דִּין ״טַיָּיל״ (כְּתוּבּוֹת ס״ב עַמּוּד א׳)
and seemingly this was because a king possesses the legal status of a gentleman of leisure (taval, Kesubos 62a);
וּמִזֶּה: דְּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ כְּגוֹן רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר שִׁילַת, דַּוְוקָא הוּא אֲפִילּוּ שֶׁכְּמוֹתוֹ שֶׁהוּא תַּלְמִיד חָכָם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בְּשִׁטָּה מְקֻבֶּצֶת
and what was taught regarding Rav Shmuel bar Shilat applies even to a scholar of his standing;
וְלֹא כְּהַ״בֵּית שְׁמוּאֵל״ רֵישׁ סִימָן ע״ו שֶׁכָּתַב דְּלָאו דַּוְוקָא
not as the Beit Shmuel (§76) wrote;
וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא דְּעוֹנָתוֹ פַּעַם אַחַת בְּשַׁבָּת, כֵּיוָן דְּהָיוּ לוֹ י״ח נָשִׁים וְנִתְחַיֵּיב לְכָל אַחַת פַּעַם אַחַת בְּשַׁבָּת, הָיָה בְּכָל לַיְלָה
and one may answer: even if a king's onah is weekly, having eighteen wives he was obligated to a different wife every night;
וְלָאו דַּוְוקָא י״ח עוֹנוֹת בְּכָל לַיְלָה, רַק לְכָל אַחַת עוֹנָתָהּ, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה הָיָה בְּכָל לַיְלָה
not that he performed eighteen visitations each night, but visited each wife on her appointed night.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם קָשֶׁה: הָא דְּ״לֹא יִהְיוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים מְצוּיִין וְכוּלֵיהּ״ (בְּרָכוֹת כ״ב עַמּוּד א׳)
And nevertheless the difficulty remains: what of the directive that scholars should not frequent their wives like roosters (Berachos 22a);
וְהָרַמְבַּ״ן קוֹרֵא לָזֶה ״נָבָל בִּרְשׁוּת הַתּוֹרָה״, וּדְעַל זֶה הוּא הַמִּצְוַת עֲשֵׂה דִּ״קְדֹשִׁים תִּהְיוּ״:
which the Ramban terms becoming a scoundrel with the Torah's permission, concerning which the positive commandment of "You shall be holy" was ordained!
אֲבָל הַקְּדֻשָּׁה הַמֻּזְכָּר בְּתַלְמוּדֵינוּ
However, the holiness (kedushah) mentioned in our Talmud (Bavli)
הוּא הַחֲסִידוּת דִּירוּשַׁלְמִי,
is the piety spoken of in the Jerusalem Talmud,
שֶׁפֵּרֵשׁ הָרַב רַבֵּינוּ נִסִּים שָׁם
which Rabbeinu Nissim (the Ran) explained there
דְּכָל מַעֲשָׂיו לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם.
as meaning that all of one's actions are solely for the sake of Heaven.
וּבְסוֹף קִדּוּשִׁין פ״ב רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳
And near the end of Kiddushin, at the beginning of 82a,
אִיתָא: "הַכֹּל לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם",
it is stated: "Everything is for the sake of Heaven,"

4.h: יִשְׂרָאֵל קְדוֹשִׁים — פֶּרֶק ד׳, סְעִיף ב׳
פִּסְקָא א׳ — דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וּזְבִיחַת הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע — Paragraph 1: King David and the Slaying of the Yetzer HaRa

The theme: King David’s absolute transcendence of carnal lust, slaying the yetzer hara through fasting, and divine assistance following human exertion. We cannot derive common guidance from King David, who designated himself a chassid (Berachos 4a), deriving no pleasure from worldly lusts like earthly kings, but acting purely for Heaven, having completely subdued his evil inclination. In Bava Batra (17a), one opinion holds that the yetzer hara had no dominion over David; the other opinion merely disputes the explicit scriptural proof, while the consensus of Avodah Zarah (20b), the Baraita in Berachos (61b), Avot d'Rabbi Natan (ch. 32), and the Zohar (Mishpatim 107b, Pinchas 227b) affirms that David's yetzer hara was slain ("my heart is slain within me", Tehillim 109:22). David achieved this by mortifying his passions through fasting; in response to his exhaustive striving, Hashem assisted him so that the yetzer had no dominion over him. Hashem does not arbitrarily strip a person's free will to turn him into an angel, for that is not the purpose of man's creation (Tosafos, Bava Batra 17a). Having attained this pinnacle, David experienced no bodily pleasure in marital intimacy, intending solely the mitzvah of the marital obligation (onah), unlike ordinary scholars whose physical indulgence would represent a departure from holiness.

p: אֲבָל הוּא הַדָּבָר שֶׁדִּבַּרְתִּי: דְּאַטּוּ אֲנַן מִדָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נֵיקוּ וְנִגְמוֹר?

דְּקָרֵי לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ ״חָסִיד״, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ לְעֵיל מִבְּרָכוֹת (ד׳ עַמּוּד א׳): ״לֹא חָסִיד אֲנִי וְכוּלֵיהּ״
Seeing that he called himself a "chassid", as we cited above from Berachos (4a): "Am I not a chassid, etc.?
שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה מִתְעַנֵּג בַּתַּאֲווֹת כִּשְׁאָר מַלְכֵי מִזְרָח וּמַעֲרָב, רַק כָּל מַעֲשָׂיו לְשֵׁם שָׁמָיִם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ לְעֵיל דְּלָא שָׁלַט בֵּיהּ יֵצֶר הָרָע.

For he did not indulge in physical lusts like the other kings of the east and west, but all his deeds were purely for the sake of Heaven, and as we stated above, the evil inclination had no dominion over him.
וְכֵן הוּא בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (י״ז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳): ״וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים: אַף דָּוִד״;
And so it is in Bava Batra (17a): "And some say: King David as well";
וּלְאִידָךְ נַמֵּי יֵשׁ לוֹמַר: דְּלָא פְּלִיגֵי אֶלָּא אַרְאָיָה מִקְּרָא דְּלָא מַכְרְעָא וְלֹא נִתְפָּרֵשׁ גַּבֵּיהּ בְּהֶדְיָא, וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם יוֹדֶה לְגוּף הָעִנְיָן;

וְכֵן הוּא סְתָמָא דְּבָרַיְיתָא בְּרָכוֹת (ס״א רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳) מֵהַאי קְרָא: דְּ״צַדִּיקִים — יֵצֶר טוֹב שׁוֹפְטָן״, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י דְּהַיֵּצֶר הָרָע מֵת;
And so is the anonymous Baraita in Berachos (61b) from this verse: "The righteous—the yetzer tov judges them", see Rashi there that their yetzer hara died;

וּבְ״אָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן״ פֶּרֶק ל״ב אִיתָא: דְּנִיטַּל מֵהֶם יֵצֶר הָרָע וְנִיתַּן יֵצֶר טוֹב מֵהָךְ קְרָא: דְּ״[וְ]לִבִּי חָלַל [בְּקִרְבִּי]״ (תְּהִלִּים ק״ט:כ״ב).
And in Avot d'Rabbi Natan (ch. 32) it is taught: the yetzer hara was removed from them and a yetzer tov was bestowed, from the verse: "and my heart is slain within me" (Tehillim 109:22).
וְכֵן הוּא עַל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בַּזֹּוהַר פָּרָשַׁת מִשְׁפָּטִים (ק״ז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳) וּפָרָשַׁת פִּינְחָס (רכ״ז עַמּוּד ב׳), עַיֵּין שָׁם.
And so is stated regarding King David, peace be upon him, in the Zohar (Mishpatim 107b and Pinchas 227b), see there.
וּבַמִּדְרָשׁ אִיתָא: שֶׁהֲרָגוֹ בְּתַעֲנִית;
And in the Midrash it is taught: that he slew the yetzer hara through fasting;
וְהַיְינוּ דְּעַל יְדֵי סִגּוּף הַיֵּצֶר בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ בְּכָל כֹּחוֹ, עַל יְדֵי זֶה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עוֹזְרוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ דְּאֵין שׁוֹלֵט בּוֹ עוֹד.
meaning that through mortifying the yetzer through human exertion with all his might, through this the Blessed Name assists him afterward so that it has dominion over him no longer.
וְעַל יְדֵי הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ הוּא שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לְכָךְ;
And through his personal striving does he merit this;
וְלֹא שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵעַצְמוֹ מְסַלֵּק בְּחִירָתוֹ מִמֶּנּוּ וְעוֹשֵׂהוּ כְּמַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת, דְּלֹא עַל זֶה הָיָה בְּרִיאַת הָאָדָם;
and not that the Blessed Name arbitrarily removes free choice from him, turning him into a ministering angel, for not for this was man created;
וְכֵן הוּא בְּתוֹסָפוֹת בָּבָא בַּתְרָא שָׁם (דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל: ״שְׁלוֹשָׁה״), עַיֵּין שָׁם.
and so it is in Tosafos in Bava Batra (17a, s.v. Shlosha), see there.
וְאַחַר שֶׁזָּכָה לָזֶה, הֲרֵי לֹא הִרְגִּישׁ הֲנָאָה גּוּפָנִית בְּכָל עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה;
And after he merited this, behold he experienced no bodily pleasure in any matters of this world;
וְלֹא כִּוֵּון אֶלָּא לְמִצְוַת עוֹנָה וּכְכָל מִצְוֹת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְאֵינוֹ כְּתַלְמִיד חָכָם דְּעָלְמָא שֶׁהָיָה בָּזֶה יְצִיאָה מִקְּדוּשָׁה:

and intended exclusively the mitzvah of the marital obligation (onah) and all commandments of the Blessed Name, not being like an ordinary scholar for whom this would constitute a departure from holiness!
פִּסְקָא ב׳ — תַּקָּנַת טְבִילַת עֶזְרָא וְהַעֲרָמַת הַיֵּצֶר — Paragraph 2: Ezra's Decree of Immersion and the Yetzer's Deceptions

The theme: Ezra’s enactment of immersion for ba'alei kerin, rabbinic fences, and the yetzer presenting sin as permissible. Even ordinary Torah scholars are not suspected of willfully violating the biblical positive command of "You shall be holy" (Vayikra 19:2) to the extent that Ezra’s enactment of immersion for seminal emissions was required solely for that; for a rabbinic decree is lighter than a biblical command. In Berachos (22a), the Gemara relates that the Sages enacted immersion to prevent sin, citing the incident where a scholar sought an unmarried woman. Rashi explains that she was an unmarried woman (penuyah), which is not biblically prohibited if not promiscuous (Rambam, Hilchos Ishut 1:4), but rabbinically prohibited under the decree of seclusion (yichud, Radbaz §225); thus an additional rabbinic fence proved effective. Unto an observant man, the yetzer hara does not entice him to commit an outright sin; rather, it blinds him to the severity of the prohibition, depicting it as permissible. Thus David and Boaz swore an oath against their yetzer (Nedarim 8a; Vayikra Rabbah 23:11; Rut Rabbah 6:4), for while one is already bound by the oath of Sinai, the yetzer deceives man into believing the act is permissible (e.g., as a concubine, pilegesh), wherefore a personal oath and Ezra's enactment proved indispensable.
וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּגַם כָּל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים לֹא חֲשִׁידוּ לַעֲבוֹר אַמִּצְוַת עֲשֵׂה דִּ״קְדֹשִׁים תִּהְיוּ״ (וַיִּקְרָא י״ט:ב׳) שֶׁיִּצְטָרְכוּ לְגֶדֶר הַטְּבִילָה
And even though ordinary Torah scholars are not suspected of transgressing the positive command of "You shall be holy" so as to require the fence of immersion;
דְּגַם תַּקָּנַת הַטְּבִילָה קַילָא מִמִּצְוַת עֲשֵׂה בְּאוֹרַיְיתָא.
seeing that the rabbinic decree of immersion is lighter than an explicit biblical positive command.
וְהַגַּם דְּאִיתָא שָׁם בִּבְרָכוֹת (כ״ב עַמּוּד א׳): דְּגָדְרוּ בָּזֶה גַּם מֵעֲבֵירָה, וּמַיְיתֵי מַעֲשֶׂה, עַיֵּין שָׁם;
And although the Gemara states in Berachos (22a) that they fenced them through immersion against sin, citing an incident, see there;
כְּבָר יִישֵּׁב זֶה רַשִׁ״י שָׁם (דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל: ״שֶׁתְּבָעָהּ״): ״אִשָּׁה פְּנוּיָה הָיְתָה, וַחֲכָמִים גָּזְרוּ וְכוּלֵיהּ״
Rashi already resolved this there (s.v. She-teva'ah): "she was an unmarried woman, and the Sages decreed, etc.";
רָצָה לוֹמַר: דִּפְנוּיָה שֶׁאֵין מֻפְקֶרֶת לֹא אֲסוּרָה מִן הַתּוֹרָה, כְּדִכְתַב רַמְבַּ״ם פֶּרֶק א׳ מֵאִישׁוּת [הֲלָכָה ד׳];
meaning: an unmarried woman who is not promiscuous is not biblically prohibited, as Rambam wrote in Hilchos Ishut (1:4);
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם מִדְּרַבָּנַן אֲסִירָא, וְהוּא בִּכְלַל גְּזֵירַת הַיִּחוּד, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַדְבַּ״ז בִּישָׁנוֹת סִימָן רכ״ה, עַיֵּין שָׁם;
nevertheless she is rabbinically forbidden, falling under the decree of seclusion (yichud), as the Radbaz wrote in his Responsa (§225), see there;
וְעַל כֵּן הוֹעִיל לוֹ עוֹד תּוֹסֶפֶת אִיסּוּר דְּרַבָּנַן שֶׁאַחַר כָּךְ.
wherefore an additional rabbinic restriction of immersion was effective to deter him.
וְיֵשׁ לְהוֹסִיף עוֹד: דִּלְמִי שֶׁלֹּא הוּחְזַק בְּרֶשַׁע, יָדוּעַ דְּאֵין הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע מְסִיתוֹ מִיָּד לַעֲבֵירָה;
And it may be further added: unto one not established as wicked, it is known that the yetzer hara does not incite him immediately to outright sin;
אֶלָּא שֶׁמַּשְׁכִּיחַ מִמֶּנּוּ חֹמֶר הָאִיסּוּר, וּמַרְאֶה לוֹ פָּנִים שֶׁאֵינוֹ עֲבֵירָה כְּלָל;
but causes him to forget the gravity of the prohibition, depicting it as no transgression at all;
דְּעַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר (נְדָרִים ח׳ עַמּוּד א׳): ״נִשְׁבָּעִין לְקַיֵּים אֶת הַמִּצְוֹת״;
wherefore the Talmud states in Nedarim (8a): "One may swear an oath to fulfill the commandments";
וּבְוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כ״ג (סִימָן י״א) וּמִדְרַשׁ רַבָּה רוּת (פָּרָשָׁה ו:ד) עַל הַפָּסוּק ״חַי ה׳״ (רוּת ג:יג): אִוֵּוסֶף דָּוִד וּבֹעַז לְיִצְרָן נִשְׁבָּעוּ;
and in Vayikra Rabbah (23:11) and Rut Rabbah (6:4) on the verse "as Hashem lives" (Rut 3:13): David and Boaz swore an oath against their yetzer;
וְאַף דְּ״מֻשְׁבָּע וְעוֹמֵד מֵהַר סִינַי״ (שְׁבוּעוֹת כ״ז עַמּוּד א׳);
even though one is already bound by the oath of Mount Sinai;
רַק הַיֵּצֶר מַרְאֶה לוֹ שֶׁהוּא הֶיתֵּר וְאֵין עוֹבֵר אַשְׁבוּעַת הַר סִינַי, עַל זֶה מוֹעִיל הַשְּׁבוּעָה;
because the yetzer deceives him into thinking it is permissible, wherefore a personal oath is effective;
וְכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ שָׁם הָיָה נִדְמֶה לוֹ דְּמֻתֶּרֶת בְּתוֹרַת פִּלֶּגֶשׁ וְכַיּוֹצֵא, וְהוֹעִיל גֶּדֶר דְּתַקָּנַת עֶזְרָא:
